As Waiqar's Deathborn Legion scourged Terrinoth and life in the cities grew perilous, citizens fled in droves, and a number of refugees set up a rough camp by the banks of the Flametail River — its position was advantageous, allowing supplies from Lorimor to easily reach the camp, and it soon gained the name Dawnsmoor, perhaps as the refugees began to see some glimmer of hope for their future. It was here that a stranger calling himself Kellos first arrived by boat, working miracles of healing among the refugees before becoming the central figure of a burgeoning cult that would grow into the Church of Kellos. Despite its relatively small size, Dawnsmoor's location on the Flametail River gives it excellent access to trade and a water route east to nearby Tamalir; the river has become something of an extension of the city itself, and many of its workers return to riverside homes each nightfall. Its rowers and fisherfolk are among the best in Terrinoth, and many a deepwater ship captain started as a Dawnsmoor river rat. Though many of the city's peoples come and go, its Elves retain a steady presence, and Elven culture has become embedded within Dawnsmoor, giving it a warm relationship with the Latari and some of the finest archers in Terrinoth — though the relationship between the city's Elves and Humans is not always smooth, with frequent trade disputes and jurisdiction conflicts. Lacking city walls, Dawnsmoor has become a waypoint for less-than-savory characters seeking rest or coin, and along with its largely itinerant populace this has given it a reputation as a place where almost anything can be purchased or contracted, no matter the legality. Some folk have relocated to smaller villages around the city, on the river, or on the moors of the Misty Plains to the south, where settlements like Brightvale spring up and slowly consolidate into hamlets, though even there an undercurrent of the disreputable can be found. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 42 The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 146

title: Dead Man's Compass
content: Dead Man's Compass This artifact is rumored to be the work of necromancers, though its origins are unknown, and arcanists have been known to use it as well. Set within a gilded frame is a glass dome, beneath which swirls a dark, viscous liquid; the bones of a Human hand float upon the liquid, bleached white save for the final joint of the first finger, which is dyed scarlet. Should someone succeed in activating the device, they may ask it to indicate a desired destination, or where something or someone may be found, and the bones will slowly form a hand that points in the right direction. Sources Magic Items, pp. 108–109

title: Death Cults of Waiqar
content: Death Cults of Waiqar The Death Cults of Waiqar were established in Tamalir by Zarihell, promising liberation both from corrupt baronial rule and, ultimately, from mortality itself, spreading Waiqar's message with ease thanks to her surpassing persuasive ability. History As the armies of Terrinoth closed in on Waiqar following his betrayal, the Tamalir cult instigated a destructive riot that drew the barons' armies away from containing Waiqar's own forces — by the time the barons arrived at Tamalir, the cult had vanished, its agents traveling throughout Terrinoth to establish new cells wherever they came to rest. Once Waiqar's armies were on the move, cult leaders kept in communication with the captains of the Deathborn Legion, particularly Zarihell and Ardus Ix'Erebus, ensuring that every major action of the Legion occurred in concert with riots in one or more of Terrinoth's cities. The resulting chaos allowed the Scourge to continue for six years before Kellos's intervention and an allied coalition finally forced the Deathborn Legion to retreat in 521. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 41–42

title: Death Knight
content: Death Knight Death knights are leagues above mere Reanimates, the very hammer of Waiqar, his hatred and will to dominate all life made manifest. Made from the dust of the most infamous and loyal of his original soldiers, they possess a degree of autonomy unknown in lesser undead, even retaining and developing personalities to a degree. Like Waiqar's elites who fought with him in the Second Darkness, death knights wear heavy armor consecrated in unholy rituals of blood; their blades are powerful relics of the events of Waiqar's betrayal, artifacts that have only become more potent after centuries of war. Riding vampiric steeds that feast upon the flesh of the living, death knights can spring suddenly out of the mists before their foes are aware of them. Sources Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), pp. 164–165

title: Deathborn Legion
content: Deathborn Legion The Deathborn Legion is Waiqar's original host of soldiers, the most infamous and loyal of whom were remade into his Death Knight elites and whose favored survivors sit at his Black Table in Zorgas, a grim mockery of the Council of Barons in Archaut. The Legion's first members were the very soldiers and bystanders who stood within sight of the Tower of Meringyr when Waiqar, having just slain Timmorran on the Night of Betrayal, swore his terrible oath to hunt down every fragment of the Orb of the Sky — the volatile magical energies unleashed by his vow conjured a freezing, poisonous tempest that snuffed out their lives on the spot, and Waiqar left the Wizard's Vale at the head of this first fearful column of shambling corpses. Waiqar discovered that the ground skeletal remains of any of his fallen Deathborn, once properly desecrated using profane rituals of his own design, could be used to animate other corpses — only a small amount of the bone dust was needed, as a single Deathborn Legionnaire could be used to raise thousands of lesser Reanimates. His forces thus grew even greater even when one of his own was laid low, though none of the resulting Reanimates were ever as powerful as his original lieutenants. It is an especially necessary duty for Waiqar's followers to collect the remains of his fallen creatures to fashion additional undead; Kyndrithul of Castle Dalibor, for one, has begun infusing living flesh with the dust of the Deathborn Legion in his experiments, a crime so grave it would mean a fate beyond death should Waiqar discover it. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 40–41 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141 Castle Dalibor (The Mistlands), p. 161 Secrets of the Grave (The Mistlands), p. 168 Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), p. 164 Zorgas (The Mistlands), p. 160

title: Deep Elf
content: Deep Elf Deep Elves are Elves who have turned their back on their cousins to more fully embrace Emorial's mission against the forces of the Ynfernael, and to redeem their name from its sullying by Malcorne, the Corrupted One. Called Deep Elves for the elaborate networks of tunnels they inhabit, they were drawn underground by the proliferation of Ynfernael gates beneath the surface, among them those found in the Dunwarr Mountains. They generally emerge aboveground only to hunt for new sources of Ynfernael power or when their crusade against the otherworldly demons forces them to do so. Their endless crusade has drained them of any dregs of mercy or compassion, as the dark powers they wield to fight the Ynfernael slowly poison their own souls in turn. Adventurers who stray into their underground lairs are lucky to escape with their lives, for the Deep Elves do not suffer trespassers or the inquisitive. Sources Life in the Mountains (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 190–191

title: Deepwood Archer
content: Deepwood Archer The Deepwood Archers, who take their name from the Deepwood trees unique to The Deepwood, were established to catch or repel any who dare try to infiltrate the forest, and are feared as few — if any — archers in Mennara can match their skill and power. Their nigh-magical longbows, formed of laminated layers of venerated wood from the cores of ancient branches, are unrivaled in strength and flexibility, drawing smoother, firing harder, and breaking less often than any other bow in the land. It is more than simply these weapons that makes the Deepwood Archers feared adversaries, though: they are trained from childhood to draw and control their unrivaled bows, so that by the time they are of fighting age, they are capable of firing at a rate and accuracy few can match, even using a bow one-third the strength. The Deepwood Archers take exceptional pride in their abilities, a confidence that often drifts into high-handed arrogance, especially when dealing with bowmen in other lands. When not serving as guards within the ranks of the Starplain Archers, the Blythwth Arethyl, or the Deepwood Rangers, they seek to participate in bowyer contests, instruct other Elven archers, and locate more impressive game than can be found in The Thalian Glades. Sources The Deepwood (The Aymhelin), p. 178 Life in the Forest (The Aymhelin), pp. 178–179

title: Deepwood Longbow
content: Deepwood Longbow The Deepwood Longbow is the signature weapon of the Latari Deepwood Archers, of little use to an amateur archer for it takes a great deal of strength and skill to use — but in the hands of a strong and experienced archer, it is a deadly weapon indeed. Its range and hitting power exceed that of mundane bows, and its construction is so solid that warping and breaking are unheard of. Sources Magic Items, p. 109

title: Deliana
content: Deliana Deliana, sister of Emperor Derisian IV of Lorimor, became regent for his infant heir Viason III after Derisian's assassination in 1312, though no hard evidence ever linked her to the killing. From the outset of her rule she was pronounced "more murderess than empress" and subjected to widespread contempt. In 1315, when Viason III was seized by persons unknown and later found in the care of a distant uncle allied with the rival House Varnii, Deliana denounced her relative as an abductor, while he claimed to have rescued the boy from "a gang of pirates." She began a military response, but Lorimor was spared civil war when the empress regent fell intensely sick and died — a poisoner in the pay of House Varnii was suspected, but never proven. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), p. 49

title: Derisian IV
content: Derisian IV Emperor Derisian IV of the noble House Harthorn was assassinated in 1312 while delivering a rousing speech from his palace balcony, struck through the heart by a crossbow bolt just as he raised his arms to accept the crowd's ovation. The speech, a polemic condemning the manipulations of his second cousin disguised as a eulogy for his recently deceased mother, was said to have been carefully crafted with the help of his sister Deliana. The assassin was never apprehended, though rumor has it that Deliana herself hired the killer — suspicion fueled by her subsequent behavior as regent for Derisian's infant heir, Viason III. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), p. 49

title: Deurg
content: Deurg Master Miner Deurg led the team from the Miners' Guild whose fateful decision, many centuries ago, to follow an unusual seam of black, obsidian-like ore toward the surface of the Dunwarr Mountains led to the discovery of what Dwarves now call the Labyrinth of Deurg in his name. After the Smiths' Guild determined that the ore, when smelted, produced a metal of unparalleled strength and resilience, Deurg redoubled his miners' efforts to excavate it — efforts that ended when the miners vanished without a trace, and the mine was sealed forever. Sources Labyrinth of Deurg (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189

title: Dhernar Keep
content: Dhernar Keep Dhernar Keep is the seat from which Baroness Magrit Kalrif rules the barony of Dhernas, sited in the shadow of the Broken Crags and overlooking the River of Sleep. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Dhernas
content: Dhernas Dhernas, the Spear of Daqan, stretches from the Hanging Woods in the west to the Whispering Forest in the east, in Eastern Terrinoth. The barony once derived great wealth from a gold mine at the base of the Shadow Peaks deep within the Hanging Wood, long since abandoned — most assume it ran dry, though others hold it haunted by the ghosts of long-dead miners guarding their glittering lode. Today Dhernas's people tend verdant farmland along the River of Sleep and harvest timber from its woodlands; Havenshyr, the barony's largest town, hosts merchants and traders thanks to its location upriver from Frostgate. Baroness Magrit Kalrif rules from Dhernar Keep, in the shadow of the Broken Crags overlooking the river — a militantly minded ruler whose spearmen and knights are respected across Terrinoth for their discipline and fine arms and armor, marching under a banner of a sword and open gauntlet symbolizing justice and mercy. Her forces have already begun deploying in response to rumors of threats from the Ru, which she eagerly anticipates joining. Dhernas is known for the wardens who protect its roads and waterways, among the safest in Terrinoth, though that claim is entirely relative. The Hanging Woods owe their name to a particularly zealous marshal, Tyrek Gorm, said to have hanged a thousand brigands from its boughs; in these times, however, the few remaining marshals are hard-pressed by growing goblin incursions and zealous devotees of dark powers on top of the ever-present bandits and thieves, and increasingly resort to bounties and hired adventurers to stem the threats. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Diggor
content: Diggor Diggor, a former guild upright, maintains the pretense of legitimate commerce in the heart of Last Haven, buying and selling what plundered wealth The Borderlands have to offer. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 212

title: Dimora
content: Dimora The Dimora are creatures born of the Aenlong, believed to cross into the world as formless elementals before building themselves out of the earth, taking on the form of stony, vaguely mole-like beings — primordial cousins to the Fae, who are at home in the air as the Dimora are in the earth. Description Elven sources suggest that by the time the Elves themselves were created, the Dimora already existed, though whether they were deliberately created by The First or were unintended manifestations of the Empyrean spheres of air and life is not a settled matter. Some scholars offer the opinion that the Fae and Dimora are experiments in the creation of intelligent life that met with mixed success, and are not quite real as mortals know reality; the Fae and Dimora are believed to be disturbing even to one another and are said to harbor mutual abhorrence, and the only known protection against either is cold iron. They are constantly shifting in density and composition, perpetually shedding the soil of their bodies and replacing what's lost with fresh loam from the ground beneath them. Their motivations for crossing into the world are generally unknown, as they rarely stray far from the rifts that allowed them entry, refuse to communicate with any creatures except the Dwarves, and seek no contact with the outside world — though they aggressively defend the land around their rifts, and tavern tales across the world tell of travelers destroyed without warning for trespassing on land the Dimora have claimed as their own. According to the Dwarves' Pact of Stonesense, the Dimora were first encountered when the earliest Dwarves fled deep into the Dunwarr Mountains to escape the dragons, and the two peoples have maintained a singular affinity ever since, one reason for the Dwarves' innate distrust of the Fae. Sources The Myths of Creation (Tales of Darkness), p. 25 Labyrinth of Deurg (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 190 Life in the Mountains (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 190–191

title: Dire
content: Dire Dire was Llovar's beloved steed, a carnivorous beast the Locust Lord had personally summoned from the Ynfernael, its harness bedecked with the heads of freshly fallen lords. When Timmorran finally struck down Llovar at the Battle of the Locusts, Dire fell alongside his master, the terrible beast's body dissolving as its energies returned to the Ynfernael. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35, 37

title: Djinni
content: Djinni The Djinni are enigmatic and deadly creatures who once ruled Al-Kalim as petty demigods from floating castles and glass citadels, before A'tar banished them to the desert, the mountains, and the sky. Table of Contents History Description Sources History Before the arrival of A'tar, the Sayr-Savim were slaves to the will of the Djinni. In great cities wrought of magic, mortals served the whims of these sorcerous creatures and lived for their amusement: Kajir, the City of Dark Dreams, traded in nightmares under the Djinn Darmarr, while Asolerr, the City of Fire, consumed a hundred Humans a day so that the fire Djinn Erfrart might bathe in molten glory. To live in such a corrupted time as a Human was to bear the mark of one's Djinn master, serve their city and their will, and wage war upon the servants of the other Djinni. Description From hidden cities and shadowy corners of the land, the Djinni weave their schemes and machinations against the Caliphate. There are many kinds of Djinni: fiery-tempered A'tari, cool and considering Maani, and flighty and fickle Falkhi, to name but a few. Djinni, like mortals, vary in power, some being ancient survivors of A'tar's destruction of their empire, others but a few centuries old, reared upon tales of when their kind once ruled the sands. Mortals know little of the Djinni themselves, though it is widely believed that once conjured into existence, they are immortal, and stories abound of the godlike powers they can wield. Striking a deal with a Djinn is a risky proposition, as illustrated by tales like that of Urnas the Unmarked, who slew a thousand mortals for the A'tari Djinn Jyrrii for the promise that no blade might ever cut his flesh again — his stone form still stands unmoving in the ruins of Jyrrii's city on the spot where the Djinn granted his wish. Even so, many mortals do not hear the warning in these stories, only the promise of power. Djinni love to meddle in the affairs of mortals, promising riches to those who do their bidding and pretending to be an agent of the Caliph or other lord to sow discord from afar. All are skilled sorcerers, but even should their magic fail them, Djinni can take on gigantic forms to dispatch foes with great falchions or daggerlike claws. Many Djinni dream of reclaiming empires, and heroes might find themselves their unwitting pawns; Djinni also lurk behind many enemies heroes might face as they unravel the threads of plots against the Caliphs. Of particular interest to Djinni is the recovery of the secrets stolen from them by the Collegiate Arcane, and as immortal beings they can spend years scheming and plotting, perhaps to recover a single artifact. Sources Al-Kalim (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 242 Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), pp. 242–243 The Great Sand Sea (Al-Kalim), p. 247 Life in the Sands (Al-Kalim), p. 248

title: Dorgan Hammerfist
content: Dorgan Hammerfist Dorgan Hammerfist is the Master Scribe of the Runescribes' Guild, overseeing the Runeforge in Thelgrim. Beyond maintaining the records of Dunwarr history and etching dragon runes into arms and armor, Hammerfist takes seriously the charge of discovering new runes or rediscovering those lost with the destruction of the Karok Doum; he is said to be seriously considering hiring a band of adventurers to travel to the Molten Heath and explore the ruins of the Dwarves' ancestral cities in the hopes of finding some ancient runecraft. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188

title: Dorgol Visoth
content: Dorgol Visoth Dorgol Visoth is one of the ruined Dwarven cities of The Karok Doum, its fallen walls and crumbling towers shattered and seared by dragon fire. Sources The Karok Doum (The Molten Heath), p. 194

title: Dragon Hybrid
content: Dragon Hybrid Dragon hybrids are cruel abominations, relics of the Third Darkness, the result of depraved experiments by the most inventive draconic invaders who required loyal servants with both the cunning of Humans and the resiliency and magic of dragon-kind — though some instead hold them to be the natural offspring of a being known as the Wyrm Queen. Largely deemed miserable failures at the time — neither as strong as dragons nor as intelligent as them or even Humans — hybrids served as foot soldiers and were discarded after the Dragon Wars ended, left to fend for themselves in the wilds of Terrinoth. Raised in the harshest life imaginable, they are vicious fighters, and time has only made them deadlier; some possess wings, others deadly talons, and still others a hint of the fiery breath associated with their larger draconic ancestors. Like dragons, they hunger for magic in all its forms, often delving into Terrinoth's many ruins or selling their swords to sorcerers and wizards willing to pay in magical artifacts. In recent years they have become more accepted in Dragonkin society, fighting alongside other Dragonkin as inheritors of Margath's legacy. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 45 Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), p. 151

title: Dragon Rex
content: Dragon Rex The Dragon Rex is the title of the most powerful dragon of her kind, who according to the histories rules over the entirety of The Molten Heath from The Heart. The current holder of the title is Shaarina. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 47–48 The Domain of Dragons (The Molten Heath), pp. 193–194

title: Dragonkin
content: Dragonkin Dragonkin is the umbrella term for dragons and the lesser draconic creatures descended from or created alongside them, including Dragon Hybrids and Salamanders, against whom the Dwarves of Dunwarr — and especially the Dwarven Dragon Hunters — harbor an abiding hatred. Sources Life on the Heath (The Molten Heath), p. 195

title: Dreamweaver
content: Dreamweaver The Dreamweavers are an order of the Latari with sanctums in the sacred vales of Lithelin, alongside the Wealdworkers. Sources Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 175

title: Duldor Deeps
content: Duldor Deeps The Duldor Deeps are a Dwarven settlement deep in the solid granite of the Dunwarr Mountains, far from the halls of Thelgrim, home to many members of the Artificers' Guild and the unofficial Alchemists' League. Within its stone halls, the Artificers' Guild tests new and inventive machinery — a constantly evolving collection of traps, locks, and deadly siege weapons — while the Alchemists' League experiments with new alchemical mixtures, acids, toxic gasses, and its infamous fire mugs and firebombs. Though these developments benefit the whole Dunwarr kingdom, they have also forced the Duldor Deeps to remain far removed from other Dwarven cities. The settlement is overseen by Chief Alchemist Freja Bjornhart and her husband, Master Artificer Stron, who fell in love after decades of working closely together despite the taboo nature of their relationship; both the Guild and the League disapproved, fearing it would compromise their members' loyalty, but in the years since it is their marriage — however grudgingly unacknowledged by either organization — that has kept the Duldor Deeps running smoothly. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 188–189

title: Dunwarr Deeps
content: Dunwarr Deeps The Dunwarr Deeps are the vast network of caverns running through the bones of the Dunwarr Mountains, domain of the Dunwarr Dwarves and home to their cities, the Hearth Road, and the passages that link them. Thelgrim is where a traveler can begin to grasp the true scale of the Deeps: the Hearth Road opens into a vast cavern filled with towering stalagmites and outcroppings of living rock that leads on to the city itself. The Deeps are also home to more perilous places, among them the sealed and forbidden Labyrinth of Deurg. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Dunwarr Guilds
content: Dunwarr Guilds The Dunwarr Guilds are the ten civic institutions around which Dwarven society in the Dunwarr Mountains is organized, each overseeing a different aspect of Dwarven life. By ancient law there can only be ten Guilds at any one time, though nothing stops an existing Guild from being broken and a new one rising to take its place; groups such as the Alchemists' League, the Fireforgers, and the Vengeance Seekers constantly scheme to supplant one of the ten. Not every Dwarf belongs to a Guild, though nearly all aspire to join one, and even the king or queen of Dunwarr is drawn from Guild ranks: each monarch is a former Guild leader, elected by vote of their fellow Guildmasters, who swears to renounce their former loyalties upon ascension (though no ruler fully escapes a little favoritism toward their old Guild). By the close of the Age of Courage, in the wake of the reconstruction of Thelgrim led by First Speaker Ingunn Vergsbold of the Masons' Guild, the Guilds had come to rule Dunwarr in all but name, and within two more decades had codified the laws governing the election of Dunwarr's speakers from among the Guildmasters. The ten Guilds are the Masons' Guild, Miners' Guild, Smiths' Guild, Artificers' Guild, Brewers' Guild, Merchants' Guild, Warriors' Guild, Rangers' Guild, Explorers' Guild, and Runescribes' Guild. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 50–51

title: Dunwarr Mountains
content: Dunwarr Mountains The Dunwarr Mountains are a bleak and foreboding range of blizzard-pounded peaks, sharp ridges of gray slate, and gnarled evergreen trees, home to the underground Dwarven kingdoms of the Dunwarr Deeps. Between the snowy crags lie high meadows of heather and gorse fed by icy brooks, and the range appears to hold nothing beyond the occasional goat or jackrabbit — the last place one would expect to find an empire. Yet travelers who follow the twisting trails into the high valleys begin to find signs of a long-lost civilization: cliffs cut too straight to be natural, sheep trails that turn out to be paved with cobblestones, craggy outcroppings that eerily resemble weatherworn faces. Following a well-worn track east of the Howling Giant Hills eventually leads into a narrow vale where, bracketed by twin waterfalls, stand the Gates of Thelgrim, heart of the Dwarven kingdoms in the Dunwarr Deeps. The range is home to the capital Thelgrim and the city of Hadranhold, the forbidden Labyrinth of Deurg and the Duldor Deeps, and to The Frontier, the sparser northern and western stretches where some Dwarves still live above ground. Sources The Dunwarr Mountains (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 186

title: Dunwol Kenn Karnin
content: Dunwol Kenn Karnin Dunwol Kenn Karnin, "The Fortress inside the Mountain," is the royal fortress of Thelgrim, standing at the far end of the city's central lake. From within its thick walls and defensive battlements — a fortress within the fortress-city — the King or Queen of Dunwarr rules from Tanngnoster's Throne. The throne and the throne room it occupies sit at the very depths of Dunwol Kenn Karnin, a final fastness for the Dwarven people in their darkest hours. At the time of the Realms of Terrinoth account, it is ruled by King Geirmund Ragnarson, whose Palace Guard is drawn from the northern barracks of the Warriors' Guild. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Dwarf Ancestral Specter
content: Dwarf Ancestral Specter The Dwarves of Dunwarr hold that the valiant Dwarves who bravely gave their lives defending their ancestral homes against the dragons of The Molten Heath have never ended their battle, even in death. Many ballads tell of the brave spirits who still roam the Heath, seeking vengeance against the dragons and others who stole their lands. One day, the Dwarves know, they will reclaim their ancestral home, and perhaps only then will these spirits allow themselves to rest. Sources Life on the Heath (The Molten Heath), pp. 195–196

title: Dwarf Guilder
content: Dwarf Guilder Dwarf Guilders are the rank-and-file members of the Dunwarr Guilds, found everywhere in the tunnels beneath the Dunwarr Mountains, since Dwarf guilds dominate society there. The ten guilds cover a wide range of knowledge, abilities, and traditions, so Guilders make ideal sources of information for visitors: depending on their guild, they can be excellent weapon forgers and repairers, decipherers of mysterious runes, or scouts and fighters. For tired adventurers, members of the Brewers' Guild tend to be the most welcome to find. Sources Life in the Mountains (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 191

title: Dwarven Dragon Hunter
content: Dwarven Dragon Hunter Dwarven Dragon Hunters are hostile, rage-filled, proselytizing zealots who give every aspect of their lives to the hunt of their ancestral foes, the dragons. They train endlessly in a specialized style of combat suited to ending the lives of dragons wherever they can be found, then make pilgrimages to places that report sightings of the beasts. When Dragon Hunters leave the Dunwarr Mountains, they aggressively try to enlist anyone they see as having the makings of an adventurer to join their quest; refusal results in a barrage of harsh and belittling insults at best, since Dragon Hunters take a dim view of anyone who doesn't hate dragons as enthusiastically as they do. In some cases, they have even taken their blade to anyone seen as "Dargeth Moni," or "friend of filth-lizards." Sources Life in the Mountains (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 191–192

title: Echard
content: Echard Baron Echard officially rules Telor, though Countess Sela's stewardship of Jendra's Harbor has granted her greater influence throughout Terrinoth and beyond, to Echard's evident frustration as he frets away his days in the crumbling halls of Grandor's Hold. Alongside Baron Gilliam Xarles of Cailn, Echard privately fears that a successful preemptive invasion of the Mistlands led by Baron Zachareth of Carthridge would make a hero of its general and upset the Council's balance of power. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143 Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 145

title: Echo Lake
content: Echo Lake Echo Lake is a placid body of water in Eastern Terrinoth, offering the region's people a peaceful respite from the bleak landscape of the nearby Borderlands. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Eddy Bloodkelp
content: Eddy Bloodkelp Captain Eddy Bloodkelp is a Gnome pirate who never had much luck due to her greater interest in nautical engineering than combat and pillaging — until her wild vision, born when her prey escaped after her ship ran aground on a huge stretch of coral reef, led her to found Tarianor, the Floating City. After Tarianor's runaway success, Eddy became richer than any pirate and, after leaving much of the daily operations to her first mate, now spends her days experimenting on new engineering projects. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 224

title: Edlund
content: Edlund Edlund, known by his soldiers as "the Mad General," commands Halfland Keep — a symptom of the faded strength so apparent in the eastern defense of Daqan. Years ago, after gaining glory in wars against the southern Orc clans, Edlund was posted to the Halfland, sure he alone could tame The Borderlands. However, during one of his first battles, a poisoned Uthuk blade pierced his side, and its Ynfernael venom caused him to become delusional. Now he is obsessed with finding the fabled Uthuk City of Blood, its existence having been revealed to him in fever dreams, and he routinely sends soldiers into the wastes, guided by his most recent vision. Edlund is continually on the lookout for those brave enough to venture deep into the Ru to Athealwel itself to locate and destroy the source of The Tangle. Sources The Borderlands (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 209–210

title: Einalf Svensson
content: Einalf Svensson Guard Captain Einalf Svensson commands the northern barracks of the Warriors' Guild in Thelgrim, overseeing the defenses of the Dunwarr Deeps and the Palace Guard that protects King Geirmund Ragnarson. He is the brother of Skirmisher Captain Lyssa Svensdottir, who commands the city's southern barracks and oversees Dunwarr military action outside the mountains. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Eleanor II
content: Eleanor II Queen Eleanor II of the Soulstone line was as renowned for her amethyst Star of Timmorran as for her exceptional battlefield prowess in the Great Goblin Uprising of 997. Her serene yet stern image can still be seen in the many gold coins minted during her reign. Sources The Rise of the Elder Kings (Tales of Darkness), p. 44

title: Elene
content: Elene Elene is a wealthy merchant whom Count Oszric Cunningham of Haverford County was forced to marry to bolster his county's poor treasury. Together the two have since funded dozens of excavations and masonry works to reclaim many of Haverford's ruins, mines, and other lost regions, though this has also disturbed hordes of goblins and other creatures dwelling within them. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Elven Boots
content: Elven Boots Whether due to enchantments cast upon them during their construction or merely because of the superlative skill of Elven cobblers, Elven Boots are renowned for providing their wearers with surefootedness, superior ankle support, and extreme comfort. An adventurer wearing them will find themselves able to hike tirelessly through difficult terrain and outpace companions in mundane footwear. Sources Magic Items, p. 109

title: Elven Loremaster
content: Elven Loremaster Elven Loremasters sing the histories of their people, relying on tempo and key to convey what words alone cannot, practitioners of Verse Magic among the Latari. Sources The Virtues of Verse (Call to Adventure), p. 125

title: Emorial
content: Emorial Lord Emorial, called Father to the Elves and Lord Protector of Light, was the husband of Latariana whose failed rebellion against The First led to the Elves' exile and imprisonment upon Mennara. Table of Contents History Legacy Sources History When Latariana's covetous longing for a Crown of Dreams and Life could not be denied, Emorial traveled to the farthest edge of creation to demand the First relinquish dominion over the Empyrean's spheres to her; they did not so much as deign to respond, leaving him humiliated and wrathful. He returned to the Elves and marshaled them in mutiny, marching his host with Latariana at his side through The Gate of Years and, unknowingly, into the Aenlong, where after countless days lost among its hazards they came at last to the glade that would become The Aymhelin and met its architect, the Yrthwright Mennara. The dragon passed down the First's judgment: the Elves were exiled from the Empyrean and imprisoned upon the mortal plane, with Latariana alone offered a terrible bargain to keep hope of return alive, at the cost of entering the Void herself. After Latariana's sacrifice, Emorial divided his host into eleven tribes and shared the Tears of Latariana between eleven Elven nobles as marks of office, directing them to lead the Elves into the future of this new world until a path back to the Empyrean was made clear. Wracked with shame, anger, and grief he could not accept for himself, he then took up his sword and left his people, journeying — the Elves say — to the Ynfernael plane to seek vengeance on the corrupting shadow that had murmured temptations to his bride. He was never seen among the Elves again. Legacy Generations later, Malcorne, chieftain of the eleventh tribe, claimed to have encountered Emorial in the Jornall Mountains where the Elves believed he had pursued the Ynfernael's servants; this Emorial supposedly revealed that the First were tyrants and that Mennara's promise to Latariana was a lie meant to keep the Elves subservient forever, charging Malcorne with revealing this truth and leading the tribes in rebellion. The Latari Elves maintain to this day that it was not Emorial whom Malcorne encountered in that cave, but a cunning demon wearing his face — a deception that set in motion The War of the Shadow Tear. The Deep Elves count themselves among those still dedicated to Emorial's true mission against the forces of the Ynfernael, in an effort to redeem the Elven name from its sullying by Malcorne. Sources The Elves (Tales of Darkness), pp. 26–27 The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), pp. 27–28 Life in the Mountains (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 190–191

title: Empyrean
content: Empyrean The Empyrean is the highest of the three Planes of Power The First conjured from the Void, a plane of perfection where the cares of hunger, age, and discomfort are utterly unknown. It is the place the Latari Elves eternally quest to return to; all Latari, wherever they dwell in The Aymhelin, fiercely guard their forests from outside intrusion lest contaminations disrupt that quest. Description Elven legends speak of four spheres existing in the Empyrean in unadulterated form: light, air, life, and dreams. The Elves themselves once dwelt wholly within the Empyrean, their spirits nourished through their relation to these spheres, until Emorial and Latariana's rebellion saw them exiled from it and imprisoned upon the mortal plane. Some mages believe Ynfernael magic to be a dark counterpart to Divine magic, holding that as the Empyrean blesses all that is good and pure in magic, so the Ynfernael empowers that which is horrid and dark. While human sorcerers pull magical energies from the Verto Magica, the Elves draw upon the Empyrean instead. As a result of Latariana's repentance and sacrifice, the stars in the night sky came into existence, the first of which, according to Elven tradition, provides a tiny but open window — Latariana's Door — into the Empyrean; a steady stream of Empyrean energy filters through this window and helps nourish the mortal realms. The Elves are uniquely attuned to such energies, which their priests can access and work into miraculous feats by following the traditions of the Path to the Stars. All four spheres are believed to have been utilized by the Yrthwrights in the creation of Mennara; according to Elven myths, Emorial and Latariana were once granted dominion over light and air respectively, and Elven priests find it much easier to access energies from these two spheres compared with those of life and dreams. Before their Fall, the original pair of Elves embodied light and air, and through Latariana's Door their descendants still have access to these spheres — learning spells that affect light and air comes very easily to the Elves, and even those who do not devote themselves completely to the Elven priesthood are able to create or extinguish small globes of light or conjure up a faint breeze. Subtle differences exist between spells that manipulate existing light or air in the Firma Dracem and those that summon light or air from the Empyrean itself: illuminating a darkened corner requires only that the Elf redirect light from one part of a room to another, a relatively minor feat, while conjuring daylight in an otherwise pitch-black cavern means summoning light directly from the Empyrean, requiring far greater strength of will and concentration. The stuff of life and dreams were greatly coveted by the Elves in the time before their Fall — Latariana's desire for power over those two spheres drove Emorial to commit his great folly. Although the Elves do not have the same connection to life and dreams as they did to light and air, Elves who join the priesthood of the Starlight Council are taught the mysteries of the remaining two spheres. With study and practice, their healers may tap into powerful life magic to perform feats of mending rarely seen outside the boughs of The Aymhelin: flesh wounds knit closed effortlessly and painlessly, broken bones come together once more as a solid whole, illnesses of body and mind can be assuaged, and unsettled emotions may be calmed, all fear and anger taken away. The dreamers among the priesthood spend most of their time in slumber, using their dreams as a portal to the Aenlong. There they may walk between worlds and catch glimpses of that which was, is, and may be; through the Aenlong as a bridge, they may also cross to the far corners of Mennara to touch the minds of other dreamers and discover their hopes, fears, and desires, working to prevent conflicts before they begin or know the precise moment to strike. Once they have tasted of the dream, however, few dreamers can bring themselves to return to the waking world for long, and most spend their eternal lives slumbering under the glimmering white ceilings of the Temple to the Stars. Since the War of the Shadow Tear, parts of the sphere of dreams have become tainted with Ynfernael energies, and on occasion a dreamer will succumb to the nightmare; the Elven high priestesses believe this is connected with the rifts between the Aenlong, the Ynfernael, and Mennara that were opened by Malcorne and his tribesmen. The Elves are not the only people to have learned to walk in dreams: long ago, the shamans of the Loth Caara were known for the realm of T'mara T'rusheen, or "walking in-between," which they may have learned from Elves who mingled with them; it is believed this in-between realm was the very same walked by the Elves in their dreams, and now the nightseers of the Uthuk Y'llan tribes stalk this realm with their own corrupted version of the T'mara T'rusheen, using the Aenlong as a place to cavort with demons before summoning them from the Ynfernael into the world. A human sorcerer wishing to create a gust of wind would simply summon forth energy from the Verto Magica, yet for an Elven wizard to do the same, they would need to summon forth a degree of air, and then a small degree of life to propel the gust; a more complex spell, equivalent in effect to a fireball created by a human sorcerer, would require input from three spheres — air to fuel the spell, light to imbue it with fire, and life to propel the missile. The more complex the spell, the more spheres must be involved in its creation. Certain magical processes that true sorcerers can undertake are virtually impossible to produce using Empyrean magic, especially those spells which directly influence water and stone — Elven priests can only accomplish such feats through indirect means, such as summoning gusts of air to blow down rocks. Illusionary magic, however, comes easily to Elven wizards: any vision can be conjured from the sphere of dreams, and by combining such visions with energies from the spheres of light and life, such illusions can even become animated and, in extreme cases, capable of interacting with the real world. Sources The Myths of Creation (Tales of Darkness), p. 25 The Elves (Tales of Darkness), pp. 26–27 Whispers of the Ynfernael (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 219 Life in the Forest (The Aymhelin), p. 178 Elven Magic (Call to Adventure), p. 127 The Empyrean Arts (Elven Magic), pp. 127–129

title: Eolam
content: Eolam Eolam, or "blue-bloods," is the name given to the High Court of Lithelin, the seat of King Aenoeth and the noble houses of the Latari — those Highborn Elves who have never left the comfort of Lithelin. An old adage among the Eolam court holds that Latariana's tears fall again due to the innumerable intrigues, plots, and jealousies that plague the court. The Eolam nominally work together to return the Elven peoples to the Empyrean or root out the vestiges of the Ynfernael from the world, while secretly working to sabotage their rivals and enhance their own influence and prestige. Sources Elves (Character Species), p. 62 Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 175

title: Erd'Lantir Urak
content: Erd'Lantir Urak The Erd'Lantir Urak, or "Water Passage," are the Orcs of The Erd Riverlands who often deal with Humans and other races. Despite its location on the Selenic Sea, their homeland is the most hospitable area of contact given that The Aymhelin, the Ru, and Zanaga border the other areas of the Broken Plains. These Orcs travel along the ever-present rivers in rough boats designed to be easily broken apart when they need to march from one waterway to the next; they are all excellent sailors, with an instinctual ability to avoid submerged threats and pull fish from the water with their bare fists. Some travel into the deeper seas beyond, and even to The Torue Albes to join exploration voyages into unknown lands. The Riverland Orcs trade with almost every other tribe and so have much to offer others coming from the sea or inland; this in turn drives many of the Orcs to visit other lands, and many go on to make new lives in the Free Cities of Terrinoth. Tales say it was an offshoot of this tribe (along with some from the Jer'Kul Urak) that many ages ago returned with a merchant ship from Al-Kalim to become the Sunderlands Orcs, where their alchemical studies of quicksilver and other rare materials have produced wonders found nowhere else in Mennara. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), pp. 198–199

title: Erenil the Swift
content: Erenil the Swift Erenil the Swift of the Latari was among the companions Glaciel Snowstar gathered on his quest to seek the dragons' aid against Malcorne and the corrupted Daewyl, helping bring about his downfall at The Battle of Enfreil. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 29

title: Erfrart
content: Erfrart Erfrart is the fire Djinn who ruled Asolerr, the City of Fire, before the coming of A'tar, bathing in molten glory as his city consumed a hundred Humans a day in its infernos. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 243

title: Eternal Fire
content: Eternal Fire The Eternal Fire was lit in Vynelvale by those who remembered tales of cleansing fire from the Second Darkness, in remembrance of that deliverance, and became the founding hearth of the church of Kellos after the first Hierophant's intercession-born ministry drew followers to it. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149

title: Eurth Kel'yr
content: Eurth Kel'yr Eurth Kel'yr, the Mistress of Bones, is one of the Ynfernael Lords served by the bloodsisters and nightseers of the Uthuk Y'llan, whose greatest followers become her mortal representatives, their interests often becoming their own. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 213

title: Eventide Forest
content: Eventide Forest Eventide Forest lies close to the Kingless Coast, a large wood said to be the abode of spirits — whether beneficent or malicious depends on the tale and the teller. Many from nearby villages travel the forest to visit the Tree of Tales, an ancient oak many throughout the region view as sacred, despite certain misgivings from the Church of Kellos. Eventide is also home to flesh-and-blood residents: a small village of Hyrrinx nestles within the forest, mostly isolated from the surrounding barony of Allerfeldt. Although in the eyes of the Citadel's law a baron has claim over all people living in their territory, the Sephone line has historically allowed the Catfolk community of Hyrrinx to govern itself independently and remain untaxed, a status quo Baroness Katrin has thus far maintained. Its northern edge falls within the barony of Telor. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Exile Peak
content: Exile Peak Exile Peak, along with Caer Loec, marks the commonly accepted boundary between northern and southern Terrinoth, and has played a part in the stories of many heroes. Wise men have come to the peak to dispense their wisdom to those heroes willing to complete its challenge. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Explorers' Guild
content: Explorers' Guild The Explorers' Guild is one of the Dunwarr Guilds, sending scouts and emissaries — and sometimes spies — into other lands to learn what the rest of Mennara is about. In the Age of Courage, the Explorers' Guild partnered with the Merchants' Guild and Miners' Guild to reestablish ties with the other Dunwarr holds once the Hearth Road out of Thelgrim had been reopened. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 51

title: Eyrat Five Fingers
content: Eyrat Five Fingers Eyrat Five Fingers is the vizier of Haruun, the one-handed lord rumored to be master of more than just his city — the thieves' guild enjoys a prosperous position under his shadowy rule. Eyrat also holds significant sway over The Thieves' Coast alongside Temoth; it is said that for every two coins that line Temoth's purse, one goes to Eyrat. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), pp. 245–246

title: Fae
content: Fae The Fae, or "fair folk," are utterly terrifying creatures of Aenlong who sometimes pass into Mennara through places where the veil between worlds grows thin, such as The Greywood. Although there are countless stories and legends that attempt to explain their true origins, if anyone knows for certain, they are unwilling — or unable — to say so. Elven sources suggest that by the time the Elves themselves were created, the Fae already existed alongside the Dimora, beings that bear resemblance to mortals in possessing corporeal bodies and thinking minds, though whether they were deliberately created by The First or were unintended manifestations of the Empyrean spheres of air and life is not a settled matter. Some scholars offer the opinion that the Fae and Dimora are experiments in the creation of intelligent life that met with mixed success, and are not quite real as mortals know reality. The Fae are at home in the air, as the Dimora are in the earth; they are believed to be disturbing even to one another and are said to harbor mutual abhorrence. The only known protection against them is cold iron, and all books pondering their existence are girded with the thick metal. From a distance, one might mistakenly believe that their form and proportions make them similar to the Humanoid races of Mennara; this is purely a trick of a mind unable to process what it is actually seeing. Their appearance varies wildly, but tales are told of distorted nostrils leading to wide maws filled with razor-sharp teeth, horns and antlers jutting at unpredictable angles from their skulls, and sightless visages whose manner of seeing without eyes is a mystery. But the thing that makes the Fae truly unique, and utterly terrifying, is the chaotic magical energy that burns inside them — it is this unpredictable, chaotic power that sends shivers up a being's spine and warns the primitive, instinctive part of their brain to run whenever they are near. Nevertheless, foolhardy mortals often seek out the Fae in places where the veil between worlds grows thin. Some are attracted by the promise of power the Fae represent; others seek to slay them for their valuable organs, used to make rare tinctures and potions; still more believe the Fae are simply misunderstood, that the right person could become the foundation of a new relationship between the Fae and Mennara. All are foolishly wrong, although it is those in the latter group who tend to suffer the most before their deaths. Sources The Myths of Creation (Tales of Darkness), p. 25 Selenic Coast (The Aymhelin), p. 177 Life in the Forest (The Aymhelin), pp. 180–181

title: Falladir Penacor
content: Falladir Penacor King Falladir Penacor ruled Talindon during the First Darkness, and Terrinoth's capital city of Archaut later grew up around his burial site. History When Llovar's Uthuk Y'llan marched to despoil the southern lands in 478, Falladir mustered his soldiers to face them but was comprehensively bested in open battle; Nashaia struck him from his steed and was poised to kill him before Prince Parren's desperate counterattack rescued the king. While Falladir nursed his wounds, the tattered remnants of his army became little more than a fugitive band, and his efforts to restore law and order to his ravaged realm continued under the constant threat of Llovar's return. Aid came the following year when a force of Latari Elves under King Triamlavar marched from the Aymhelin to fight alongside the Penacors, beginning a great tradition of alliance between Humans and Elves against Ynfernael threats; together their combined forces relieved Thelgrim from siege, and Falladir and Triamlavar later joined Timmorran's campaign against Llovar. In 487, the Host of Thorns fell upon an army led by Falladir and his sons at The Ashen Field; though Falladir's sword nearly cleaved the head from Melinesh, Llovar's numbers, magic, and malice proved too great, and the three Penacors lay dead upon the field by the day's end, along with the soldiers who had followed their banner. Only a small group of survivors led by the young Baron Daqan escaped the slaughter. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35–37 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Farrendon
content: Farrendon Farrendon was the surviving son of King Jerlon Penacor and Queen Riya, sharing none of his father's frailties and displaying more of the robust spirit associated with the Penacor line after his brother Farrengol was executed for banditry and his father died a lonely, unmourned death as the King of Grief. Sources Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), p. 33

title: Farrenghast
content: Farrenghast Farrenghast was once Prince Farrengol Penacor, elder son of King Jerlon Penacor and Queen Riya, executed with his outlaw followers for unspeakable crimes; the dark oaths they swore the night before their hangings allowed them to rise again as revenants. Table of Contents History Description Sources History Lacking any parental hand after his mother's exile and his father's descent into melancholy, Farrengol fell in with coarser members of the royal household guard, who taught him to ride and fight but also brought him along on secret raids of far-flung farmsteads; on his sixteenth birthday, humiliated by a court jester's verse, he fled the castle with his friends and turned to outlawry around the wild lands of Nerekhall. Roving knights eventually tracked the outlaws down and took Farrengol and his companions alive; imprisoned in the Tower of Nerek to await his father's judgment, Farrengol discovered a Daewyl portal hidden in the tower and an Ynfernael shade within, to whom he promised fealty if only it might somehow grant him freedom. King Jerlon nonetheless condemned his son to death, and the outlaws' bodies were cast into the mires of the northeastern swampland — but the shade had not forgotten its promise, and invigorated by dark magic, the bodies of Farrengol and his companions rose from the swamp to resume their old crimes. With the loot and weapons they captured, they set up a fastness of their own in a ruined keep among The Misty Hills overlooking the marshes that had been their grave, and Lord Farrenghast, as the foul wretch came to be known, went on to terrorize the surrounding lands with his skeletal followers. More than a century passed before a valiant band caught Farrenghast, believed at the time to be his end — though accounts persist of him haunting Terrinoth several times since. During the First Darkness, before his own fall into undeath and betrayal, Waiqar — then still the Sunderland general Waiqar Sumarion — grew bored of his duty relieving the siege of Thelgrim and devised his own campaign against the undead forces of Farrenghast, banishing the undead horde in a great success. Description Taking the name Farrenghast, the prince and his fellow revenants were perhaps the first time such fell creatures had banded together in a mass of evil. Over time, their foul essence seeped into the earth itself and made it as vile as they, darkness that may have called to The Mistlands, which absorbed the region into itself. Few today dare speak of Farrenghast or the Lords of Bilehall except when heavily inebriated. Sources Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), pp. 32–33 The Rise of Llovar and the Uthuk Y'llan (Tales of Darkness), p. 33 The Misty Hills (The Mistlands), p. 162 Secrets of the Grave (The Mistlands), p. 168 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 36–39

title: Felfrost Spike
content: Felfrost Spike On the slopes of Felfrost Spike in the Dunwarr Mountains, the Deeplord brothers Bran and Ordan faced the Dragonlord Gehennor during the Third Darkness, part of the Deeplords' furious counterassault against the draconic horde that sent armies of dragon hybrids deep into the halls of the Dunwarr Deeps. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 48

title: Feral Dragon
content: Feral Dragon Dragons are perhaps the most powerful beings in all of Mennara; no one knows where they come from or what their purpose is when they embark on their destructive flights, but all possess an insatiable appetite for magical objects and can detect magic from hundreds of leagues away. During the Third Darkness, also known as the Dragon Wars, dragons plundered countless holdings for their magical artifacts, leaving other treasures untouched or burned to ash. Feral dragons — uncultured, savage remnants of that war — occasionally appear and rampage across Terrinoth as little more than violent beasts. Suffused with magic, they are very nearly impossible for the average soldier to kill, and even mighty heroes must rely on runebound shards to have any hope of slaying one; as dragons possess both flight and a mastery of magic great enough to level cities, a sighting is a sure sign to flee, for rarely does anything but doom follow. Sources Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), pp. 151–152

title: Feredel
content: Feredel The Feredel were one of the eleven Elven tribes among whom Emorial divided the Tears of Latariana. The Feredel sorcerer Keldarim joined Glaciel Snowstar's quest for the dragons' aid against Malcorne and the Daewyl, helping bring about his downfall at The Battle of Enfreil. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 29

title: Ferrox
content: Ferrox Ferrox are humanoid creatures found in The Mistlands, with pale green skin over powerful muscles and membranous skin stretched between their arms and torsos that allows them to glide, giving them a very bat-like appearance when extended. Their arms terminate in wicked, hook-like claws, and their mouths are filled with razor-like teeth. Vicious and savage, these creatures are only dimly intelligent, and easily dominated by certain dark magics. Those unfortunate enough to encounter ferrox in the Mistlands rarely live to tell the tale, and rumors persist that those who survive their bite slowly transform into one of these foul creatures. Sources Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), p. 165

title: Finwalyn
content: Finwalyn The Finwalyn, or "forest children," are the animated trees of The Aymhelin, first awakened when the ancient songs of the Latari — sung for their own comfort upon first falling to Mennara — unexpectedly stirred an unknown joy in the mysterious hearts of the young forest, giving movement to root and bough and trunk. Through the practice of the Wealdcallers, these young saplings grow taller and stronger over time, eventually becoming the mighty Forest Guardians that are sometimes seen marching to war alongside the Latari. Sources Wealdcallers (Elven Magic), p. 129

title: Fireforgers
content: Fireforgers The Fireforgers are one of several groups in Dunwarr society — alongside the Alchemists' League and Vengeance Seekers — that strive for the power and prestige of a full Guild and constantly scheme to supplant one of the ten existing Guilds, who in turn work tirelessly to maintain their own authority. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189

title: Firestone Furnace
content: Firestone Furnace The Firestone Furnace is an immense, ancient kiln forged of an unnamed alloy, sitting deep below Hadranhold in the center of a lake of boiling magma; only the wondrous nature of its construction keeps it from melting into slag. Dwarves of the Smiths' Guild reach the Furnace across obsidian bridges reinforced with inlaid runes that ward off its ferocious heat, using it to forge ores into wondrously pure ingots and to craft the hardened, dragonfire-resistant steel that makes up the Gates of Thelgrim. The Furnace is kept running night and day, year-round, overseen by the Greathammer Hafnir Irontamer, whose ceaseless dedication is driven in part by the knowledge that if the Furnace is ever left empty for too long, it could heat beyond its own melting point and collapse into the magma below — a tragedy that would devastate the Smiths' Guild and the entire Dunwarr kingdom. Sources Hadranhold (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188

title: First Fall
content: First Fall First Fall is a sheltered port town southwest of Lithelin on the Selenic Coast, built around a natural lagoon and bulwarked by Elven masons and elemental sorcerers millennia ago. The town is almost immune to the battering winds, deep swells, and forceful riptides of the open ocean, and almost all seaborne trade with the Elven empire in The Aymhelin comes through First Fall before being carried north and east by carts towed upon well-maintained cobblestone roads. Sources Selenic Coast (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Flayed Kindred
content: Flayed Kindred The Flayed Kindred do not covet rulership of the Ru like the Gore Claws; instead they seek only to make themselves closer to the power of the Ynfernael realm, descended from Llovar's inner circle. Their warriors purposely maim themselves, pouring demon blood into the wounds, so that they might be remade as more than mortal. The witches and warlocks of the Flayed Kindred hold many of the keys left in the wake of their master's demise, including those believed to open the gates to the Black Citadel. The quest for the Black Citadel remains a constant among the tribe; many of its witches and warlocks believe that if it can be found, Llovar himself might be returned to the world. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 211

title: Flesh Ripper
content: Flesh Ripper Flesh rippers are the heralds of the Uthuk armies: packs of these slavering beasts lead the charge into battle with savage roars and screams, their blood-red sinew, bulging muscles, and bony, armored hides leaving little doubt as to their demonic ancestry. As large as full-grown lions, flesh rippers tower over most prey, yet their size belies their speed — racing across the ground on all fours, these vicious beasts can easily catch a knight on horseback, while soldiers on foot have no hope of outrunning them. When flesh rippers catch their foes, they truly live up to their name; even a single such monster will paint the earth red as it rends apart its prize, and when one sees a single flesh ripper, others are never far behind. The wrangling of flesh rippers is no easy task, as Uthuk beastmasters' countless old scars and missing limbs can prove. Witches and warlocks use blood sacrifice to lure the flesh rippers from the tempestuous heart of The Ru and cage them with sorcerous power; the demons are then branded with the N'klashth, or bloodmark, making the covenant of ownership complete. Once the creatures are broken to the will of the Blood Coven, beastmasters use barbed whips to corral them, and when the horns of war sound and the beasts are let loose, their instincts take over. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 214–215

title: Fleshwright
content: Fleshwright Fleshwrights, also known as Flesh Moulders, are practitioners of Necromancy who affect dead tissue in horrific ways, altering raw tissue into twisted new shapes through their fell arts. Additional limbs, insectoid eyes, and elongated fingers with venomous nails are only some of the less horrid transmutations they can achieve. Some even use their powers on themselves, constructing bizarre but deadly forms to better serve Waiqar the Undying One. Sources Secrets of the Grave (The Mistlands), p. 169

title: Forest Guardian
content: Forest Guardian Forest Guardians are the largest of the animated trees of The Aymhelin, unnerving to behold at any time but especially in combat. They march forward with a fearless abandon, lashing out with their "legs" and using the dense gnarl of their branches and trunks to smash and crush anything that stands before them. Forest Guardians are preternaturally strong, have the inherent resilience of a dense hardwood tree, and act with an efficient brutality borne of beings who may be utterly divorced from the constraints of traditional mortality. They almost never stride beyond the great forest, though some have been seen in large battles against Broken Plains Orc invaders or Uthuk raiding parties. The groves between the palace and walls of Lithelin were originally created for the Forest Guardians, who lend aid in defense of Caelcira. A younger and lesser cousin of the Forest Guardian is the Aymhelin Scion. Sources Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 175 Life in the Forest (The Aymhelin), p. 179

title: Forest of Fangs
content: Forest of Fangs The Forest of Fangs is a stretch of jungle in Zanaga that grows thick and twisted with Tarakhe's power, where Singhara Hunter parties stalk the darkness seeking out the plague god's followers, the roars of leonine warriors and hisses of their serpentine enemies echoing among the blister-covered trees. To the north, where the Skyscar Peaks plunge into the Forest of Fangs, lies the Chasm of Despair. Sources A New World (Zanaga), p. 253 The Lost Expedition (Zanaga), p. 255

title: Forge
content: Forge Forge is one of the eight Free Cities of Terrinoth, located at the base of the great mountain shrine of Yrthwright's Forge west of Tamalir, one of many cities dedicated to the art of the smithy. History Forge was once an ancient Dwarven stronghold before Humans became part of it during the Third Darkness, when its conqueror, the Dragonlord Avox, demanded it produce greater quantities of arms and armor with metal from its mines. That destructive occupation means much of Forge is relatively new, including many homesteads built to house the enslaved Humans, many of whom reside in Burrow Town, a village clinging to the slopes of the mountain and cutting into the rock itself, though others are scattered across the city mixing with Dwarven enclaves. Even though Humans and Dwarves fought as one to rebel against the dragons and now hold yearly celebrations honoring the event, tensions between the two peoples remain high: Dwarves displaced during the war returned to find Humans seemingly everywhere, outsiders almost as unwanted as any other invader, while Humans see the Dwarves as callous about their former slavery and unappreciative of their own efforts to help end the draconic occupation. Description Despite the tensions, Forge includes perhaps the finest smithies in Terrinoth. Deep in the mountain, primal flames burn hot and pure enough to allow the crafting of incredible weapons and works of art; only a few aspiring apprentices eager to learn the secrets of forging metal are taken annually, and some wait long years for an opening. No small amount of business comes from travelers seeking to have broken blades or holy relics restored in the mountain's cleansing fire. Due to its smiths' exceptional metalworking skills, Forge uniquely avoids sending tithes of labor, gold, or crops to the Daqan Lords, providing only arms and equipment instead. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), pp. 146–147

title: Fort Rodric
content: Fort Rodric Fort Rodric stands in the Ashen Hills of Pelgate, constructed following the Dragon Wars to honor the hero Rodric, its namesake. The fortress has never been taken by force, nor even attacked, and after long years of peace its garrison is severely undermanned — yet it remains of vital importance, guarding the route past the Broken Crags against invasion from the east. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Forthyn
content: Forthyn Forthyn, the Last Civilized Land, marks the furthest north boundary of Terrinoth, stretching from the Broken Crags to the Blind Muir Forest. Its people are hardy folk, toughened by harsh northern winters. The Free City of Frostgate falls within Forthyn's bounds, a source of some tension since the barony cannot officially command the fiercely independent Free City, though Frostgate relies on Forthyn's goodwill for its imports. From her home at Highmont, Baroness Adelynn personally oversees the raising and training of Forthyn's famed rocs — massive eagles domesticated long ago and bred as war mounts — a duty her lineage has carried out for centuries; she provides trained rocs to certain other baronies under longstanding traditions and alliances, and great artificial eyries in the mountains house expert breeders and trainers who have adapted to the thin, cold mountain air over generations. Recently, unknown thieves have made several attempts to steal rocs, including hatchlings and eggs, thwarted so far by the roc-masters and the baroness's men-at-arms. The persistence and resourcefulness of the thieves in such perilous terrain has led some Forthyners to fear a darker power lies behind the rustling — for the mighty rocs to fall into the hands of Terrinoth's enemies would bode ill for the Land of Steel. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Fortuna
content: Fortuna Fortuna, Lady of Luck and Trickery, is a favorite deity of adventurers, whether she smiles on them or not tending to determine whether they emerge from a dungeon alive and treasure-laden, or end up in some ogre's larder. History Fortuna's devotees say she once wandered the realms of Lorimor as one of the most infamous connivers and rogues of the age, and that she once tricked an entire duchy into believing she was its long-lost ruler — ruling for a year and a day before vanishing along with the treasuries of the once-smug nobles who had praised her heritage and manners. This exploit and hundreds more earned Fortuna countless toasts in countless taverns, and in time people began speaking a prayer to her before throwing dice, deceiving marks, or taking the stage. Perhaps her ascension to divinity was her finest performance and greatest trick of all. Worship There is not so much a clergy of Fortuna as there are supplicants seeking her blessing. There are no known shrines or churches erected in her name; instead, gambling dens set out offering bowls to lure her favor, and as soon as eyes turn away, the proffered coins seem to vanish, Fortuna always quick to accept her due. The arrival of her desired blessings is, appropriately enough, more a matter of luck. Sources Spirits of Power (The Strength of Devotion), pp. 123–124

title: Fraternity of the Mountain
content: Fraternity of the Mountain The Fraternity of the Mountain is a monastery of sorts in Trelton. When smiths and metalworkers first approach the city seeking entrance to learn from its masters, the Fraternity examines them as to the truthfulness of their statements: if their hands are calloused, if they do not flinch in the face of a roaring furnace, if they find nothing wrong with soot and ash, then they are accepted and given access to its forges. Food, bed, shelter, and companionship are made available to anyone who stokes fire and counts the moments of their life to the pounding rhythm of the hammer on the anvil, regardless of their origin. Many have journeyed countless leagues to gain entry, practice their craft, repair priceless relics, and create their own masterworks. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 224

title: Fredric
content: Fredric Baron Fredric rules Kell, a barony whose valley farms keep it fed while producing enough surplus to trade with the nearby Dunwarr and Joulnar Dwarves and the barony of Dhernas. A rich trade in timber and iron keeps coin flowing into Fredric's vaults, though it seldom rests long before he puts it to use for the betterment of his people and lands. Fredric is a descendant of Roland of Kell, who is said to have slain High Lord Margath at the culmination of the Dragon Wars, and many see that same nobility in Fredric. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Free Cities Elf
content: Free Cities Elf Free Cities Elves, a voluntary colloquialism, are Elves who have forsaken their tribe — or were born to Elves who did — choosing to live alongside the short-lived races as urbanites, most commonly found in cities such as Dawnsmoor and Tamalir. The term can also include Elves whose bloodline has mingled with that of Humans. Sources Elves (Character Species), p. 63

title: Freja Bjornhart
content: Freja Bjornhart Chief Alchemist Freja Bjornhart oversees the Duldor Deeps together with her husband, Master Artificer Stron, head of the Artificers' Guild presence there. They fell in love after decades of working closely together, though their relationship was taboo from the very beginning: the Artificers' Guild feared Stron's loyalty to his wife would weaken their dominant position, while the Alchemists' League saw Freja's love for her husband as fraternizing with the enemy. Both received stern admonishments to avoid the other, which they dutifully acknowledged and immediately ignored. In the years since, neither organization has been willing to admit that Freja and Stron's marriage is what has kept the Duldor Deeps running relatively smoothly; instead, the Guild and League argue over which organization the couple's eventual children will join. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189

title: Frest
content: Frest Frest, Barony of the Usurped Throne, is unique among the baronies in being ruled not by a hereditary noble but by a first-generation baroness, Harriet the Willful. Some decades ago, Harriet was a simple carpenter; when the previous baroness abruptly abdicated, Frest fell into chaos that hit the peasantry hardest, until Harriet united her fellow peasants against the bickering nobles and assumed leadership herself. Since her appointment by the will of the people, she has ruled magnanimously from Aerendor Keep: farmers keep what they like and profit from the rest, and Frest has the lowest taxes in all Terrinoth. Its people till the fields and hunt and gather from the serene Applewood Forest, though all know to avoid the Bloodwood on the barony's eastern edge, where the vengeful Elves have claimed few victims in recent years. The other barons did not take Harriet's rise well and went to war with Frest; the war raged for years until she was finally accepted onto the Council of Thirteen, largely because the war was going poorly for the other barons. Even now the barons fear their own people might follow Frest's example, and as Harriet ages and succession is discussed, some worry that her daughter inheriting the throne would legitimize a precedent for commoners to ennoble themselves or unseat barons entirely. Wary of open action against Harriet risking another war or inciting revolt elsewhere, Baroness Magrit of Dhernas and Baron Gillian of Cailn have instead begun quietly seeking information that might turn Frest's people against their ruler. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Frostgate
content: Frostgate Frostgate is the northernmost of the Free Cities of Terrinoth, the entry point to the wild, untamed lands of eternal winter, and one of the few places in the region where raw materials can be procured and goods manufactured. Barely a city for much of the year, Frostgate is more a seasonal community whose fortunes rise and fall with the coming of winter: summers see it almost emptied as its denizens leave to hunt and farm, but as the cold returns the city blooms, filling with hunters and trappers, herders and farmers, tradespeople and their retinues who return to meet and conduct business. The natural riches of the Blind Muir Forest, the shipping lane of the River of Tears, and the abundant minerals of the nearby Shadow Peaks feed its trade. During the crowded winter months, fields of yurts press against the city walls and industry pushes on into the night; in this season Frostgate can rival Tamalir in size, with temporary theaters, courts, temples, and shops erected within days, and the revelry can be heard long before the city is seen. The Northern Tribes perform rituals at this time to ensure good harvests and successful hunts, greatest among them the Trials of Frostgate — contests using sacred elixirs and herbs to access ancestral spirits, in which contestants enter spirit planes to face challenges of strength, cunning, and courage against aspects of mighty animals; those who succeed are marked with tattoos proclaiming them Champions of Frostgate. Before venturing into the North, bands of travelers tend to assemble in Frostgate, the sole community in the region outside a small colony of Latari among the evergreens, and the Champion's tattoo can be a sign to such groups that its bearer has adequate prowess for the dangers ahead. Frostgate falls within the bounds of the Barony of Forthyn, which leads to some tension: the barony cannot officially command the Free City and its fiercely independent ruling council, but Frostgate relies on Forthyn's goodwill for its imports. The city also lies at the far end of the Pilgrim's Trail through the Shadow Peaks, where survivors of the trail's trials often travel onward to find the warmth of Frostgate's chimneys, roasting tundra boar, and Dwarven ale. Caravans travel between Frostgate and Thelgrim in the Dunwarr Mountains, inspected along the way by Bradha the Shield, commander of the garrison at the Gates of Thelgrim. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 144–145 The Free Cities (Terrinoth), pp. 147–148 The Mountain Gates (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Gafford
content: Gafford From a distance, travelers might think there is a violent war underway within Gafford, due to the clouds of smoke and rising flames. Yet, upon entering it, they soon realize that these are simply the product of the locals going about their daily business on Garnet Island. Gafford is a city of magical alchemists and base chemists; there is no potion or concoction that cannot be found here in abundance, many first developed in one of its heavily fortified mixing dens. The Hollow Woods bordering the city to the north is one of the only places where certain ingredients can be procured, making it the principal destination for students of botany (and, unsurprisingly, poisons). What the residents cannot cultivate locally, they send their ships to procure, making Gafford one of the primary importers of rare minerals and other ingredients from the icy wastes of Isheim and elsewhere. Gafford's production is not limited solely to potions of strength or vigor, but also includes flash bombs, grenades, smoke bombs, shells, and all manner of bizarre reagents. The infamous concoction known in Terrinoth as "Lorimor Fire" is a major export, though the locals keep a much more highly refined and powerful version for special buyers. Explosions are the most common occurrence on the island, requiring a dedicated water brigade to handle the innumerable blazes. For those more inclined toward the pleasurable things in life, Gafford is also renowned for its taverns, masters of alchemy often being masters of the cask and keg as well. Many of its more legendary spirits are the result of accidental mixtures of alchemical and alcoholic brews, some never having been successfully replicated despite years of efforts.
