A magnum of the legendary Crimson Gaff, in particular, can fetch an ogre's weight in gold, and there are frequent expeditions to locate the crate of Queen's Kiss that went missing somewhere on the way to Tamalir. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 224

title: Gardens of Tarn
content: Gardens of Tarn The Gardens of Tarn are a sacred forest admired for its natural beauty in Southern Terrinoth, from which the people of Otrin respectfully gather rare herbs; under barony law, felling a tree there is punishable by death. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 137–138

title: Garnet Island
content: Garnet Island Garnet Island rests to the west of Alben, bounded by the Cerridor Sea to the south and the Bright Sea to the north, offering a natural break for travel through The Torue Albes. Among its verdant forests are several small settlements, which mostly conduct illicit smuggling, and only one city, Gafford, which most visitors would consider more an explosive testing ground than a proper city. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), pp. 223–224

title: Garnott
content: Garnott Garnott is a coastal city bordering the Burning Bay, far to the south of Dallak in The Torue Albes. Life in Garnott is martial and rigidly controlled, making it the perfect home for the premier military training school in the islands: the Torue Albes War Academy. Garnott is much more defensible than most locations in the Torue Albes: to the north of it lie the Azure Peaks, and would-be seagoing invaders need to get past the Narrows of Gracor, where many a ship ends up smashed against the rocks. Watching over the city are all manner of magical charms, said to be the last gift of a Lorimor emperor whose son perished when his ship was dashed upon the banks. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 223

title: Gaspard Bay
content: Gaspard Bay Gaspard Bay is a young, rising hero ennobled for his efforts fighting with the eastern Hernfar garrison, who desperately wishes to be given lordship over Roth's Vale — not just for himself, but to fulfill a promise made to his ancestors. Sources Roth's Vale (The Mistlands), p. 162

title: Gates of Thelgrim
content: Gates of Thelgrim The Gates of Thelgrim are the outer fortifications guarding the approach to Thelgrim, banded and reinforced steel doors nearly two hundred hands high, shaped in the silhouettes of two mighty Dwarven warriors standing back to back. Crafted from bands of hardened steel joined by hundreds of rivets and stamped with runes of endurance — steel forged using the Firestone Furnace and resistant to dragonfire — the doors bear the dents and scars of dozens of assaults as testament to their indestructibility. Hidden defenses are wrought into the gates and surrounding cliff faces: murder holes and disguised firing ports let unseen Dwarven guardians rake attackers with crossbows, ballistae, and firebombs, hidden sally ports allow counterassaults, and the water of the falls above can be redirected to flood the entire approach valley. The Dunwarr Dwarves maintain only a light garrison at the Gates, since even a few score soldiers can hold them for weeks while Thelgrim itself is merely a day's march away; the garrison is commanded by Bradha the Shield, who also inspects the caravans traveling up from Frostgate to trade with Thelgrim's merchants. Sources The Mountain Gates (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 186–187 Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Gauntlets of Power
content: Gauntlets of Power These magical gauntlets resemble mundane armored gauntlets, save that they are forged from thick slabs of black iron rather than thin sheets of bright steel. Their origin is unknown, though the brutal aesthetics suggest Orcish work. There is a practical frugality to the enchantment cast upon them: they store energy from the blows that strike them, then release it when striking back, allowing an adventurer in melee combat to inflict stunning blows. Sources Magic Items, p. 109

title: Geirmund Ragnarson
content: Geirmund Ragnarson King Geirmund Ragnarson is the King of Dunwarr, ruling from Tanngnoster's Throne within Dunwol Kenn Karnin in Thelgrim. His Palace Guard is drawn from the northern barracks of the Warriors' Guild, commanded by Guard Captain Einalf Svensson, who also oversees the defenses of the Dunwarr Deeps. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Geist
content: Geist Geist, one of the ten sons of Baron Deiterhelm of Otrin, had long ago left the barony and renounced any claim of inheritance to study in Nerekhall — what he learned in that cursed city is unknown, but two years into the War of Ten Brothers he returned at the head of an army of vicious Ferrox raised from the wildlands of the Broken Crags. History Geist quickly crushed one of the three warring alliances of brothers, personally slaying two of his half-siblings; the others decried him as a "Usurper" and pled for aid against his obviously evil magics. When the barons refused to answer the call of the Warden of the Citadel, Lady Anastel of Kellos's Order was anointed Justicar to combat the threat, retrieving the Shield of Coals and marching alongside a force of zealous priests and knights — but Geist's magics warned him of her approach, and he ambushed her forces as soon as they crossed the border. Most who did not fall were corrupted and turned by the foul bite of the ferrox, barely one in four living to return to Vynelvale; Anastel was not among them, and Geist pried the Shield of Coals from her dead hands. Geist seemed unstoppable, and in the winter of 1662 he laid siege to the fortress of Black Rock, a victory that would let him dominate the Morshan River all the way from Skydown to the Aymhelin forest. Bearing the Shield of Coals, he used its power to summon a hail of fire onto the defenders, and it fell to the free city of Riverwatch to stand alone against him — the entire company of the Riverwatch Riders mustered forth during the coldest days of Deepwinter and attacked his flanks before his horde, deployed to surround Black Rock, could turn to meet them. The ferrox faltered before the steel-eyed riders and fled with Geist to the frozen river, but as they crossed, the Shield in Geist's hands began to glow with searing heat; with a howl he dropped it on the ice, which melted away in the face of Kellos's wrath, and in moments Geist and his ferrox drowned in the freezing water. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 52–53

title: Gentias II
content: Gentias II Emperor Gentias II of House Harthorn brought Lorimor's civil war to an end at the Battle of Ranthor Bay in 1490, having inherited the most powerful faction in the conflict but facing the risk of being overwhelmed should his enemies ever unite against him. History Gentias II is believed to have won the war more through a clever propaganda campaign than military genius, compromising a number of messengers employed by his rivals and tasking them with relaying deliberate misinformation about various factions' intentions and movements — at three points during the war, armies clashed under the mistaken impression that they fought House Harthorn, when in fact they battled allied forces. He finally ended the war at Ranthor Bay, a minor feature on the island of Alben, by convincing two of his three remaining rebel cousins — the heads of House Varnii, House Crosta, and House Ferastii — that the third wished to combine their might there; in reality his own force was encamped around the cliffs, and as his enemies landed and assembled their troops, he launched a surprise assault, burning their boats with magical fire as massed ranks of archers rained bolts on their soldiers. By the battle's end, the head of House Crosta was dead, the head of House Varnii in chains, and the head of House Ferastii fled into exile. The Battle of Ranthor Bay marked the end of the war, but is also considered the end of the Lorimor Age — the empire would endure, but never again dominate the continent as it once had. In its aftermath, House Harthorn liquidated House Varnii's possessions in The Torue Albes, a betrayal that provoked the revolts leading to Lutetia Dallia's founding of the independent Queendom of the Torue Albes. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), pp. 49–50

title: Georgiana Delacroux
content: Georgiana Delacroux Baroness Georgiana Delacroux of Frest abdicated her position in 1827 to marry the Orc chieftain Lazra the Huntress, a scandal that baronial politics treated as great sport. Since Georgiana had no children and had failed to name an heir before her departure, her various relatives vied to control the barony, a conflict that ranged between court politics and occasional clashes between loyal supporters — until the carpenter Harriet Laurel grew tired of the fighting and led a rebellion that ultimately won her the barony instead. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 53

title: Ghur'zhun Urak
content: Ghur'zhun Urak The Ghur'zhun Urak, meaning "Lightfoot Tribe," are a clan of pathfinders, rangers, and mountain dwellers who claimed The Ghur Highlands as their own many centuries ago. Members secretly roam down from the mountains to harass anyone near the edges of the Plains — all in defense of their own lands, if challenged — ambushing Elven and Uthuk scouts alike, laying traps along the well-worn paths, and sneaking into any nearby villages to steal horses, supplies, weapons, and especially casks of Elven wine. The Elves answer by sending rangers to hunt for the Ghur'zhun Urak, but the Orcs are generally gone long before they arrive; repercussions from the denizens of the Ru, however, can be savage. The Orcs still view these battles as necessary to judge the growing threat of the Darklands, for it is as the watchmen of the Plains that the Ghur'zhun Urak are most valuable to the Broken Plains. Their tall homelands allow the Ghur'zhun Urak to act as a kind of early warning of impending attack from outsiders. From their mountain perch of Urakuhl, the Lightfoot Tribe has an eagle's eye view of the vast terrain surrounding the Plains. On the occasions that the Ghur'zhun Urak ride down from the mountain and call their rival tribesmen to arms, petty squabbles are quickly put aside so that the Plains can be defended against any attackers. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 199

title: Giant Snake
content: Giant Snake The jungles of Zanaga host a great many types of snakes, and the larger they are the more deadly they become. Some seem to have no upper limit on their size, and tales speak of entire groups of adventurers swallowed up in fanged, cavernous maws. Sources Life in the Jungle (Zanaga), p. 258

title: Giant
content: Giant Few have seen these huge, lumbering creatures and lived to speak of it, for their raw strength is enough to crush entire bands of soldiers like lesser beings would swat away flies. Many are as old as the hills, with reclusive natures, and immediately see outsiders as enemies. Despite the relatively small sizes of its islands, much of The Torue Albes is still unexplored, and giants can still be discovered within enormous underground caverns or wading through deep marshes and lakes in search of prey. Luckily, giants are relatively slow, though their long strides more than compensate; cunning or magic are the weapons of choice when facing these immense foes, for attempting to match them in brute strength or common weaponry likely ends with a fresh gravestone to mark yet another adventurer's death. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 225

title: Gildspar
content: Gildspar Gildspar was an outcast Dwarven smith who forged the Mirror Hammer, a masterwork born from a vision that drove him into seclusion to complete it. Struck by a vision of the weapon and its function, Gildspar spent ten long years journeying to the heights of a mountain range where a perpetual lightning storm — said to be created by a floating runebound shard — blasted away at the jagged peaks. He set metal ingots where lightning could strike them and infuse them with its energies, then carved runes upon each ingot for every bolt of lightning that found its mark, before finally putting the metal, charged with the energies of a thousand bolts, to the forge. Sources Dwarves (Character Species), p. 65

title: Gilliam Xarles
content: Gilliam Xarles Baron Gilliam Xarles rules Cailn, the Scarred Crossroads, from Castle Tagis, overlooking the abandoned, dragon-scarred Thelsvan Plains. Together with Baroness Magrit Kalrif of Dhernas, Xarles has quietly begun seeking information that might turn the people of Frest against Baroness Harriet, wary of the risks of open war. He is also, alongside Baron Echard of Telor, privately fearful that a successful preemptive invasion of the Mistlands led by Baron Zachareth of Carthridge would make a hero of its general and upset the Council's balance of power. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143 Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138 Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 145

title: Glaciel Snowstar
content: Glaciel Snowstar Glaciel Snowstar, son of the chieftain of the Nivalis, the tenth Elven tribe, refused to give in to despair after witnessing firsthand the devastation wrought by Malcorne and the corrupted Daewyl during The War of the Shadow Tear. History Glaciel rescued his father's Tear of Latariana and resolved to travel to the Yrthwrights' own home to ask the dragons for their guidance and help in defeating the corrupted Elven chieftain. Along the way, he gathered companions to his cause: High Priestess Celeneth of the Salish, the Feredel sorcerer Keldarim, Erenil the Swift of the Latari, and others — the extent of Glaciel's adventures and the exploits of his companions have made their way into countless lays still sung in the verdant settlements of The Aymhelin. The dragons, whom The First had tasked with preserving the world, seemed to anticipate his coming, but remained aloof even as he begged them for aid, rebuffing his appeal as the Elves' own burden to bear and warning that intervention would one day force the tribes to pay a terrible price. Glaciel would not leave, and accepted the dragons' terms; he and his companions returned to rally their respective tribes with a flight of dragons at their back. On the Plains of Enfreil, they fought a final battle against Malcorne, and in the world's most desperate hour their combined forces ultimately achieved victory and struck down the dark Elven lord. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 29

title: Gnome Minstrel
content: Gnome Minstrel For reasons still unknown, a large number of Gnomes from across Mennara make their way to The Torue Albes each year, often in the early days of summer, spending months traveling from island to island surviving on their wits and their skills with the lute, pipes, small drums, and their own musical voices to pay for lodgings and meals. Some of these bards display arcane abilities, leading scholars to believe there could be something in the Albes that calls to their magical nature. Whatever the reasons, these entertainers can be found playing in almost every tavern, inn, and other gathering place in the area. They tend to pick up all of the local gossip as well, and can be excellent sources of the latest word on the streets — for a price, of course. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 226

title: Goblin Witcher
content: Goblin Witcher Few would consider goblins intelligent enough to utilize magic, yet some of exceptional cleverness have managed not only to discover their sorcerous abilities but to harness them to a degree. Adventurers who come across witchers often take them for mere goblin leaders, learning better only when bolts of energy are hurled their way. Like all goblins, witchers are cowardly and avaricious, but their access to dark magics lets them brutally slay foes from whom most of their kin would flee in terror. Sources Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), pp. 152–153

title: Goblin
content: Goblin Goblins are smelly, small, and decidedly cunning when they wish to be, standing on average shorter than a Dwarf and usually possessed of a cowardly personality — a valuable instinct in a place where death is quick and painful. Lacking any real sense of courage or tactics, goblins usually attack in packs, raiding and stealing what they can before being chased off by the local guard or an angry farmer with a pitchfork. Though they seem like they should be easy to exterminate, goblins are quite difficult to root out fully from their caves and homes, breeding quickly in the dark and rebuilding their numbers within months. In their willingness to steal anything of value — mostly food and shiny things — they are more a resilient, destructive pest than anything, though they must not be underestimated, for cowardly as they are, they can be turned into a semi-coherent fighting force by a leader offering the right motivation, such as Splig, King of All Goblins. Sources Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), p. 152

title: Goldhall
content: Goldhall Goldhall is the traditional seat of the Sephone family, the castle from which Baroness Katrin rules Allerfeldt, the result of several hundred years of construction and a legacy of her line. High spires, grand halls, vast storehouses, and immense barracks make Goldhall one of the most impressive castles among all the baronies, a veritable fortress defending the whole of Allerfeldt. In recent times it has taken on a more administrative than military role: its vast complexes, immense library, and facilities to host dignitaries and state functions make it a frequent first point of contact for important diplomatic actions, the site of many a treaty and declaration of war, while the Weeping Causeway serves as a mustering ground for Allerfeldt's combined armies. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 142

title: Golreth
content: Golreth Golreth is the prophet from whom the Gore Claws, the largest and most aggressive of the Uthuk Y'llan tribes, claim descent. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 211

title: Gor-Bor-Gor
content: Gor-Bor-Gor The angry pounding of drums is the language of the ape god Gor-Bor-Gor, largest of all Zanaga's primates, cousin to the Monkey God — a creature of rage and strength, to whom reckless warriors give prayer before battle or mimic his war cries to frighten their foes. Legend has it that Gor-Bor-Gor resides within the Spire, a peak that looks like a great slumbering ape when the sun sets upon its slopes, waiting for a great champion who will break the stone chains that hold him and thus loose him upon all of Zanaga. Unsurprisingly, many of Zanaga's Orcs worship Gor-Bor-Gor and are constantly trying to wake the creature so he might begin his rampage against civilization, bringing living sacrifices to the Spire or seeking out groves of blood-red fruit said to stir rage in even the most placid soul, hoping enough of it might tempt him down from his Spire. Sources A New World (Zanaga), p. 254

title: Gore Claws
content: Gore Claws The Gore Claws are the largest and most aggressive of the Uthuk Y'llan, their filed nails and crimson-stained hands marking them out among their kin, descendants of the prophet Golreth. They keep the legends of Llovar and the Ynfernael masters alive; centuries of secrets have been recorded by Gore Claw witches on piles of flayed skin. As the self-proclaimed inheritors of the Locust Swarm, the Gore Claw witches and warlocks strive to unite the tribes and use their mastery of demon magic to build armies, forge alliances, and further the revenge of their people. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 211

title: Gorhta Tamer Uglar
content: Gorhta Tamer Uglar Gorhta Tamer Uglar stands at Skorn's right hand as leader of the tribal council of Mag Ugluk Urak and Master of Obedience, overseeing all the various forms of beast training. Terse, humorless, and abusively insulting, Uglar is almost universally despised by the rest of the tribe — and if not for his amazing abilities in beast-taming, he would have been murdered by his brethren decades ago. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Grand Cathedral of Kellos
content: Grand Cathedral of Kellos The Grand Cathedral of Kellos stands in Vynelvale, built by successive hierophants over the centuries into a structure to rival the greatest castles of the Daqan Lords, with wings, halls, and bastions added over generations. Behind its towering walls, hundreds of initiates silently tend gardens and fields, while innumerable scribes spend the years copying holy texts and other rare documents. It is here that the Priests and Knights of Kellos are trained in the greatest secrets of their god. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149

title: Grand Duke Consino
content: Grand Duke Consino Grand Duke Consino established himself as ruler of The Torue Albes by 1505, having first won a victory against the small army House Harthorn sent to maintain Lorimor's interests after the islands revolted against the liquidation of House Varnii's possessions there. Downfall Knowing that Lorimor could conclusively beat his remaining army should it turn its attention to reconquest, Consino set about repairing his reputation with the empire, trying to arrange the death of the famed mercenary captain Lutetia Dallia — who had conducted a brilliant campaign on his behalf to win him the throne — in order to curry favor with House Harthorn. Lutetia survived several assassination attempts and captured and interrogated one of her intended killers, refusing him mercy until he revealed who had paid him; she then led a force of elite mercenaries to storm Consino's castle and threw him into his own deepest oubliette, taking the throne of the Torue Albes for herself. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), p. 50

title: Grand Temple of A'tar
content: Grand Temple of A'tar The Grand Temple of A'tar in Irram is tended by Sun Priestess Sharish, and holds the tomb of the first Caliph — once each Caliph's reign is over, their body is brought here baked in clay, so it might be entombed within their likeness forever. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 245

title: Grandmother Tree
content: Grandmother Tree The Grandmother Tree stands in the Greatwood, a sacred symbol of prosperity for the barony of Rhynn, which honors it with a tree upon its heraldry. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Grandor's Hold
content: Grandor's Hold Grandor's Hold is the crumbling seat of Baron Echard of Telor, where he frets away his days while Countess Sela's stewardship of Jendra's Harbor eclipses his influence. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Gravia Kein
content: Gravia Kein Warden Gravia Kein has for the last two decades executed the orders of the Daqan Lords after they return to their baronies, overseeing the day-to-day matters of state at the Citadel until the next year's gathering, serving Terrinoth with honor and passion. In recent years, Kein and the officers under her command have seen fit to employ itinerant adventurers and other mercenaries to deal with matters ranging from suspected dragon cults to Ferrox swarms, goblin raiders, and fugitive necromancers. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 142

title: Great Goblin Uprising
content: Great Goblin Uprising The Great Goblin Uprising of 997 was a conflict during the Time of the Elder Kings in which Queen Eleanor II distinguished herself for her exceptional battlefield prowess, wielding her amethyst Star of Timmorran. Sources The Rise of the Elder Kings (Tales of Darkness), p. 44

title: Greatwood
content: Greatwood The Greatwood is a forest in Northern Terrinoth, home to the Grandmother Tree, a sacred symbol of the barony of Rhynn's prosperity honored in its heraldry. Its southern portion falls within the barony of Telor. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Greigory
content: Greigory Baron Greigory rules Rhynn from his seat at Castle Arhynn, an older man with a thick white mustache who projects an air of leisurely sophistication, at odds with the militant persona of his close ally Baron Zachareth of Carthridge. In many ways Greigory rules Rhynn as the greatest among equals, his authority more precarious than most barons' since Rhynn's politics are split between his inner circle and the many lesser nobles grown wealthy from the Carthmount silver trade. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Greyhaven Wizard
content: Greyhaven Wizard To the outside world, the wizards of Greyhaven are a reclusive bunch, hiding away in their towers to augur the arcane truths of rune magic away from prying eyes; to those who have fought beside them, they are some of the mightiest allies one could ask for. Those wizards with the aptitude and dedication to see combat are known as battlemages, often deployed to support battalions of infantry and knights, defending themselves with runic bolts of fire or lightning, or channeling rune magic into the ground to raise limbs of soil and stone against their enemies. For many adventurers, though, it is their knowledge that is most desired — scholars of Greyhaven are privy to the mysteries concerning the runebound shards and how they came into the world. Sources Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), p. 153

title: Greyhaven
content: Greyhaven Greyhaven is one of the eight Free Cities of Terrinoth, home to its hallowed university — though few realize it was the town that came first and not the other way around. History Though records of its founding are sketchy, most hold that it was Timmorran himself who founded the northern city, perhaps for refugees lost in the wilderness and those seeking to forget the horrors of the First Darkness, though he may have had other reasons for the location. The nearby confluence of two rivers and the town's accessibility made it a natural trading nexus, and it grew over the years into a cosmopolitan center of learning; legends grew alongside it, such as that the Fae were repelled by the nearby waters, or that the undead could not be raised within its gates. Though never proven, these tales drew those of an arcane bent, and the greatest university in Terrinoth was built here solely to study magic, with deep dungeons excavated for dangerous experiments and the wisest wizards from every court and city recruited as instructors and masters. Description Greyhaven now boasts the foremost magical colleges in all of Terrinoth, perhaps in all the world, its wizards famed for their wisdom and dedication to the magical arts. The Daqan Lords draw their battlemages from Greyhaven, and most current knowledge of rune magic originates from it; the university possesses the largest number of known runebound shards of any city in Terrinoth, frequently used in its mages' more exotic and powerful experiments. Its colleges cover all the arts, from history to farming to rhetoric, though most specialize in aspects of magical lore and practice — attending means long days of study, long nights of reading, and frequent practice sessions that only rarely lead to catastrophic explosions, while graduation ensures a long, if dangerous, career. Even those not attending often travel here just to observe lectures and practice with adepts. The Pilgrim's Trail through the Shadow Peaks lies not far from Greyhaven. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), pp. 147–148 Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Grotesque
content: Grotesque The power of the Blood Coven can twist and torment Uthuk warriors, but it can also grant them great power, should they be strong enough to bear its blessing. Grotesques are monstrosities, each a uniquely horrid form that only vaguely resembles the Uthuk they once were. Having offered themselves up for sacrifice to the Blood Coven, they have hacked off limbs, given over eyes, or even torn out their own beating heart in hopes of receiving the witches' Ynfernael blessing. If the Blood Coven approves of a warrior's offering, they might be rewarded and their mangled body remade anew: bone ridges begin to cover their body, their hunched back becoming a forest of razor-sharp spines while their muscles swell and distort under their pale flesh, and gone are the vestiges of mortality from their face, elongated fangs and glowing red eyes marking them as the beast they have become. In battle, the grotesques are the lumbering elite of the Uthuk tribes, many rising to become warlords of their own raiding armies or wasteland fortresses. Horrendously strong in combat, grotesques can rip a person apart with their bare hands, carve them up with their bone spines, and even fling bone shards from their fists to fell enemies at a distance; few bother to carry weapons or wear armor, as their demonically transformed bodies are able to take and dish out enormous amounts of punishment. A supernatural terror clings to them, making combatants who wouldn't normally flee before their grotesque size and appearance find their nerve undone, and this panic can become infectious — just one of these towering horrors can send a disciplined force into a rout, and grotesques grow intoxicated upon the outpouring of fear, rising to a killing frenzy as they fall upon their fleeing foes. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 215

title: Guild Hall (Thelgrim)
content: Guild Hall (Thelgrim) The Guild Hall is the seat of the Dunwarr Guilds in Thelgrim, standing on the shore of the city's central lake opposite Dunwol Kenn Karnin. Its imposing facade displays one ornately decorated pillar for each of the ten guilds that make up the heart and soul of Dwarven society. Unlike the sober quiet of the King's fortress, the Guild Hall is a raucous and lively place, where the heads, sub-heads, and representatives of each guild spend hours in spirited debate, each trying to further their own guild's interests and expand their authority; more than once these debates have devolved into brawls that force the king's own representatives to haul guild members outside and toss them into the lake to cool off. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Gurak Tol
content: Gurak Tol Gurak Tols are territorial, six-legged lizards native to The Broken Plains that jealously guard their homes, whether a warren, isolated cave, or valley — instinctive behavior that has made the creatures invaluable allies for the Orcs, especially Mag Ugluk Urak. Swift, sure-footed, and incredibly aggressive by nature, Gurak Tols do battle and defend themselves with vicious attacks from strong tails tipped with a bone club or spikes. Generally they rely on their teeth and the claws on their lead fore-legs at the start of combat; once their prey is wounded and the Gurak feels bold enough to take its eyes off their enemy, though, they swing their massive tails with the force of a trebuchet's ball upon the target's skull or spine. Their tails also allow them to perform a ranged attack when an Orc Outrider provides suitable ammunition. Gurak Tols have been captured and "domesticated" into becoming Orc steeds, but there are still many wild herds that occupy the Broken Plains. While the Orcs actively seek out Gurak Tols for new mounts, they also protect the great lizards from outsiders lest their numbers diminish. Sources Life on the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 202

title: Gyrar Abyss
content: Gyrar Abyss The Gyrar Abyss is a great crack in the Darklands of The Ru, home to hidden, shadowed chasm cities and the Well of Sins. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 211

title: Hadranhold
content: Hadranhold Hadranhold is a Dwarven fortress-city in the Dunwarr Mountains, built into Mount Valborne, that grew from a lonely watchpost into a fortress and then a city over the centuries. From the surface, all that can be seen of Hadranhold is the original stone tower and battlements built into the mountain's peak; the Rangers' Guild maintains the tower as its unofficial headquarters. The rest of the city lies deep below the surface, reached from the tower by a single stone staircase of thousands of steps, and has been carved into the caverns of the Deeps much as Thelgrim was. Unlike Thelgrim, Hadranhold lies close to the molten heart of Mennara, and members of the Smiths' Guild and Artificers' Guild have moved there in numbers to take advantage of the abundant heat for smelting and forging; the lower city, unlike the cold and lonely upper fortress, has become a bustling city of skilled artisans. Deep below Hadranhold sits the Firestone Furnace, an immense, ancient kiln forged of an unnamed alloy standing in the center of a lake of boiling magma. Every winter solstice, Dwarves of the Rangers' Guild from across the Northern Coast make the trek to Hadranhold for Wintersmeet, the Guild's traditional week of feasting and fellowship. Sources Hadranhold (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188

title: Hafnir Irontamer
content: Hafnir Irontamer Hafnir Irontamer, called the Greathammer, oversees the Firestone Furnace beneath Hadranhold, keeping it running night and day, year-round. Horrifically scarred and hairless, Hafnir has had almost every inch of his stout body seared or burned in his labors. His level of ceaseless dedication is about more than just pride: should the Furnace be left empty for too long, it could heat beyond its own melting point and collapse into the fiery magma below, a tragedy that would have horrible ramifications for the Smiths' Guild and the entire Dunwarr kingdom. Sources Hadranhold (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188

title: Halfland Keep
content: Halfland Keep Halfland Keep, the largest of Daqan's border keeps, stands at the crossroads between west and east in The Borderlands, where many heroes gain their first taste of what the Ru has to offer. It is a thriving fortress, and villages cluster close to its walls for protection despite the keep's dark reputation. A posting here is a common punishment among the armies of Daqan, and lords who wish to rid themselves of troublesome adventurers or rivals might write them a letter of introduction to the keep's commander, Edlund, or grant them a commission to become defenders of the eastern realm. Sources The Borderlands (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 209

title: Halgir Son of Grom
content: Halgir Son of Grom Halgir Son of Grom was a Dwarven Deeplord of Thelgrim who argued during the First Darkness that the Dwarves should accept their share of responsibility on the battlefield against Llovar, while the other Deeplords, having promised the continued use of Thelgrim to their Human and Elven allies, refused to commit their own troops beyond self-defense. History Halgir's pleas eventually persuaded the Deeplords to send Dwarven troops to reinforce Timmorran's army as it made its stand against Llovar's Host of Thorns at the Battle of the Locusts, arriving unexpectedly from Thelgrim. When Kul the Serpent's assault broke through to Timmorran's position, wounding King Triamlavar, an enraged Halgir challenged Kul to face his axe — but for his bravery, the Deeplord's own skull was pierced by one of Kul's bodkins, a sacrifice that nonetheless helped exhaust Kul's efforts and allow Timmorran to survive the onslaught. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 36–37 Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Hall of the Ancestors
content: Hall of the Ancestors The Hall of the Ancestors is the repository for the Dwarven dead, located even deeper beneath the heart of Thelgrim than the Runeforge. Within the hall are seven hundred and thirty-four unsealed sarcophagi, the temporary burial grounds of the newly deceased; the corpses are left to decompose there for seven hundred and thirty-four days, after which the bones are transferred into a miles-long collection of antechambers shared, in the loosest possible sense, with their families or guilds. Only the monarchs of Dunwarr are given prestigious, individual burials, interred in large, elaborate tombs of sealed metal and stone whose tableaus and intricately engraved poetry relate the legends of their reigns. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 188

title: Halls of Phetra
content: Halls of Phetra The Halls of Phetra are a collapsed ruin in the south of Roth's Vale, once a temple to a god no being now living remembers. The halls are still filled with a light that can banish fell shadows. Sources Roth's Vale (The Mistlands), pp. 162–163

title: Hamzah the Pridelord
content: Hamzah the Pridelord Hamzah the Pridelord is the Singhara lion god of war, a megalithic cat who prowls the vast plains of Zanaga and lairs in the world cave beneath Singhavrem. The Singhara proudly roar out their devotion to him when they embark upon the hunt or charge to war, and legends tell of how, when he is needed, Hamzah bounds forth to join the fray. Heroes who earn the respect of the elder Singhara might be honored with the chance to enter the great cat's lair and take a strand from his mane; when woven about weapons or armor, it is said to increase their strength tenfold. More nefarious individuals may instead try to slip past Singhavrem's temple guards and into the sleeping cat's lair, where it is said he rests upon a mountain of bones tangled with treasures. Sources A New World (Zanaga), p. 254

title: Hanging Woods
content: Hanging Woods The Hanging Woods lie to the west of Dhernas in Eastern Terrinoth, a heavily forested and largely unsettled territory that owes its name to a particularly zealous marshal, Tyrek Gorm, said to have hanged a thousand brigands from its boughs. An abandoned, possibly haunted gold mine that once brought Dhernas great wealth lies at the base of the Shadow Peaks deep within the wood. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Hardell
content: Hardell The city of Hardell, on Ulthik Isle, saw its beginnings when a wizard tinkerer was banished from his home in Terrinoth for the excessive destruction caused by his inventions. History The exiled mage made his lonely way to the isle, expecting nothing but an uneventful life — that was, until he accidentally discovered the plentiful raw materials under his feet. Soon he was smelting and forging items of metal and magic never before imagined; word spread of his creations, especially to nearby Trelton, and similarly eccentric and outcast inventors eagerly crossed the Winnowing Straits to join him. Soon, a series of forges and smelters rose up, and the city of Hardell, named to honor the wizard, was born. Description Hardell is a place of destructive wonders, where the wizard's genius is now recognized in full. His masterpiece is perhaps the Rune Cannon, an arcane weapon that magnified the strength of runic bolts a hundredfold, capable of blasting apart rock and heavy fortifications with ease. In addition to the Rune Cannon, an endless number of devices and mechanical contraptions can be found here, many singular creations awaiting someone to fully appreciate their potential, or figure out how to use them. Adventurers seeking specific items or modifications to existing ones for their latest quest are always welcome in Hardell, for its inhabitants always appreciate a good challenge. Sources The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 225

title: Harridan the Stalker
content: Harridan the Stalker Harridan the Stalker, ally to Arachne, is the patron of spies and assassins in Zanaga. A bird goddess, she has lived in Zanaga for generations beyond count, able to take the shape of a woman or a mighty mountain condor. Her followers include members of all races, though unlike those of Arachne, they serve her willingly, hoping to help protect Zanaga from evil gods and the greed of mortals. In this way, Harridan tempers Arachne's hunger for power, and she often uses the spider queen's network for her own. Adventurers could find themselves called upon to aid the bird goddess's agents or even become agents themselves, traveling the land and fighting against those trying to destroy or exploit Zanaga; the reward for such service is often information, for Harridan knows many secrets indeed, including the paths to places long forgotten by mortals. Sources A New World (Zanaga), p. 255

title: Harriet the Willful
content: Harriet the Willful Harriet the Willful is the Baroness of Frest, a former carpenter named Harriet Laurel who rose from the peasantry to unseat the barony's squabbling nobility and take its throne. Overview Some decades before the present day, the baroness of Frest abruptly abdicated her position — Realms of Terrinoth records this earlier abdication as that of Baroness Georgiana Delacroux, who left to marry the orc chieftain Lazra the Huntress — leaving no named heir and throwing the barony into chaos that fell hardest on the peasantry, as various relatives vied for control. When the other barons treated the resulting succession conflict as sport, backing rival claimants, the carpenter Harriet Laurel grew tired of the fighting and led a rebellion of Frest's peasants and merchants. History The rebellion grew quickly in strength under Harriet's capable leadership; before the neighboring baronies could muster their levies, she had eliminated most of the legitimate claimants and taken control of the barony's major towns. She and her generals ruled under siege for fourteen years, repulsing every attempt by the other barons to put down the "peasant uprising." Eventually the barons relented and treated with her at Archaut, and under the neutral eyes of the Warden of the Citadel she was granted title and domain of Frest, becoming Baroness Harriet the Willful. The other barons then went to war with Frest outright, a conflict that raged for years until Harriet was finally accepted onto the Council of Thirteen, in no small part because the war was going badly for her opponents. Since ruling from Aerendor Keep, Harriet has governed magnanimously, letting farmers keep what they like and giving Frest the lowest taxes in Terrinoth. Though other barons resent her common heritage, none can argue she has not ruled Frest justly. As she ages, the question of succession looms: should her daughter inherit and establish a hereditary line, some barons fear it would legitimize a precedent for other commoners to ennoble themselves or challenge baronial rule, and Baroness Magrit Kalrif of Dhernas and Baron Gilliam Xarles of Cailn have begun quietly seeking ways to turn Frest's people against her rather than risk open war or provoking revolt among their own peasants. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 52 Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Haruun
content: Haruun Haruun, the City of Pillars, is a vizier city-state of Al-Kalim lying largely beneath the Celestial Mountains, ruled by the vizier Eyrat Five Fingers. A vast stone bridge leads visitors into a gaping hole in the cliffs and down deep into the cool ground. Carved by captive sand crawlers, Haruun is a warren of quarters and districts beneath cavernous stone vaults, dotted with shafts of light and fields of glowing moss. Haruun is often called the City of Outcasts, for it is here where many of Al-Kalim's unwanted come to make their way; Eyrat does little to counteract this reputation, and it is rumored that the one-handed lord is master of more than just his city — the thieves' guild enjoys a prosperous position in this shadowy place. Within its cavern roof hangs the Tower of Knives, where the Hysshari Brotherhood trains its acrobatic killers. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 245 Life in the Sands (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Haunters' Wood
content: Haunters' Wood Haunters' Wood is a petrified forest cloaked in eternal shadow within The Ru, marking the resting place of the Seven Sinners, wizards of singular and cruel power driven from Daqan by righteous citizens. Slain by their servants and buried in shallow graves, the wizards defied death, rising up as great and evil oaks — sentient trees that exude darkness, making the wood an ideal hunting ground for the Ru's predators. Illusions of safe haven conjured by the Seven lure prey, including travelers, into the wood, where their spilled blood can feed the trees. The wealth of the Seven remains, too, tangled about their roots, just waiting for those skilled enough to traverse the midnight forest and battle its many monsters, and then the trees themselves. Sources The Ru and the Darkness (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 210

title: Havenshyr
content: Havenshyr Havenshyr is the largest town of the barony of Dhernas, hosting merchants and traders thanks to its location several leagues upriver from Frostgate. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Haverford County
content: Haverford County Haverford County lies within the barony of Allerfeldt, ruled by Count Oszric Cunningham and his wife Elene. The county has a poor reputation despite strong, intermarriage-bolstered relationships with the other counties, owing to a generations-long pattern of each Cunningham ruler bringing a new, usually unproductive obsession to the throne — half-finished buildings and failed alchemical experiments dot its landscape. Oszric and Elene have since funded excavations and masonry work to reclaim many of the county's ruins and lost regions, disturbing hordes of goblins and other creatures in the process. In 1627, an earlier Countess Cunningham of Haverford joined the counts of Allerfeldt and Rostum in destroying Waiqar's Raven Horde at Carum's Cross, calling down a bolt of lightning to burn the Raven Priest to cinders when he attempted to resurrect his fallen troops. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 52 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Hearth Road
content: Hearth Road The Hearth Road is the underground passage that stretches seven leagues from the Gates of Thelgrim to the heart of Thelgrim itself, wide enough for five wagons to travel abreast. Intricate runework runs the length of its walls — a history of the Dwarven people for those with the ken to read it — and every inch of the road is smooth and polished, the work of Dunwarr Dwarves who can shape and sense stone and metal by touch. Before the Third Darkness the road ran unbroken into the great cavern housing Thelgrim, but after Gehennor's dragon hybrids used the Hearth Road to reach the city's heart, the Dwarves cut a deep chasm across that side of the cavern; only a single arching bridge now links the Hearth Road to the city, guarded by further gates and battlements. In the Age of Courage, First Speaker Ingunn Vergsbold of the Masons' Guild had the Miners' Guild cut the chasm crossing that still carries the road today, reopening the link between Thelgrim and the outside world and setting off the rise of the Dunwarr Guilds' political power. Sources Thelgrim (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 51

title: Hearthlord
content: Hearthlord The Hearthlords are the jarls of the Weik, each controlling a city or town along The Raider's Coast of Isheim with a fleet to prowl the waters beyond the cliff tops and sheltered bays. Their title has been handed down from the first captains since Lagrul the Red led the Weik's twelve pirate fleets to Isheim's shores. Each year upon the longest day, the twelve Hearthlords convene as the Reaver Council in Lagart to spit upon the broken statue of Nordros and reaffirm their mastery over their land. It is each Hearthlord's duty to dig the roots of their city deeper into the soil of Isheim than their predecessor, clearing its forests, harvesting its wildlife, and raising new settlements — a success that has led to trade wars among them over resources like ice-blood, fought with manipulation and politics, or raids and open warfare. Sources The Frozen North (Isheim), pp. 232–233 Lords of the Hearth (Isheim), p. 234

title: Hector Ysphane
content: Hector Ysphane Count Hector Ysphane was an avid collector of rare artifacts whose greatest prize, three dragon eggs discovered in a cave on his lands, led to the destruction of his own Tairnheath Castle in 1701. Ignoring the frantic advice of his court wizard, Ysphane displayed the eggs in a place of honor directly next to his great hall's hearth. The wizard fled that very night and carried the story to Greyhaven; when no news came from Tairnheath after a month, he enlisted a group of adventurers and returned to find the castle reduced to a burned-out husk, with seemingly no survivors. A dragon hatchling, already twice the size of a horse, had made its lair in the cellar beneath the castle; the adventurers slew it at the cost of the wizard's hand, and picked over Ysphane's treasury as payment before returning to Greyhaven. What became of the other two eggs remains unknown. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 52–53

title: Hedge Wizard
content: Hedge Wizard Hedge wizards, or "magicians" as they are sometimes known, are self-taught or informally-trained sorcerers who never passed through the disciplined schooling of an institution such as Greyhaven. They tend to be treated with suspicion, which is not altogether unwarranted: many such vagabonds took to the life because it was easier than the stringent standards expected of the magical schools, while others may have been expelled for carrying out their own unsupervised investigations into magic, including occult practices. The magic of such wizards is therefore wilder and more inclined to dangerous side effects than that of their more disciplined classmates, though more scrupulous hedge wizards also take up adventuring, usually on their own personal quests to uncover strange magical practices or lost magical artifacts in the wild places of Mennara. Sources The Arcane Arts (The Magic of Mennara), p. 116

title: Helka the Bold
content: Helka the Bold Helka the Bold is the legendary mother of the Dwarves and first of the runescribes, a skilled miner who traded her sight for the secrets of the dragon runes to save her dying daughter Valnir, and who led the Dwarven armies against the dragons in the last stand at Black Ember Gorge. Table of Contents History The War of Fire Sources History When the rents left by the Shadow Tear spilled otherworldly energies across the world, the Dwarves are said to have sprung forth from the rocky, flame-wreathed crags of The Molten Heath, scraping out a miserable existence amongst the basalt outcroppings and lava flows of the Heath's heart, hunting the Salamanders that basked along the shores of the molten lakes and foraging for shar-roots and lindengrass beneath the rocks. Amongst them lived Helka, who struggled to raise her daughter Valnir alone after the death of her mate. When Valnir grew sick from the ash-laden skies and all knew she would soon die, Helka refused to accept this, journeying with her daughter deep into the heart of the Heath to find the great and terrible beings that made their lairs in the tallest fire-mountains and demand their aid. The journey was long and perilous, but finally Helka found a vast cave atop the tallest mountain, within which dwelled a monstrous serpent with silver scales and golden eyes. Fearlessly, she faced the dragon and demanded it help save her daughter's life. The dragon gestured to claw-carved runes covering the cave walls: it would let her use them to save her daughter, but in turn it would take Helka's sight, so that she could not pass that knowledge on to others. The Dwarf agreed, and the dragon showed her which runes could be spoken to heal her child — they would be the last thing she saw, as its wondrous visage grew in brilliance and seared her eyes. The dragon left, and Helka spoke the words of power to cure Valnir; then, feeling her way to the cave wall, she began memorizing by touch the shapes of the other runes carved there. When Helka returned to her kin, she scratched every rune she could remember onto a slab of basalt, and as the Dwarves began to unlock these secrets, the days of their primitive existence ended. The runes contained the secrets of magic, metalworking, farming, and masonry. With this knowledge, the Dwarves traveled from the fire-scorched heart into the green prairies encircling the Heath, building great cities of brass and basalt they called The Karok Doum, "gift of dragons" in the Dwarven tongue. For many years they worked to build a realm of stability and peace, as Helka continued to study the secrets of the runes and Valnir became a great leader of her people, but the peace was not to last. The War of Fire The dragons of the Molten Heath grew to resent the Dwarves, calling them thieves who had stolen draconic knowledge, and eventually they went to war. Though the Dwarves fought valiantly, such a war could only have one outcome; one by one their cities burned, and the shattered remnants of their armies made a final stand at Black Ember Gorge, refugee caravans fleeing behind them into the hills and plains beyond while the dragon armies circled before them. Though old and frail, Helka led a final army against the dragons, telling Valnir to lead the remainder of their people to safety; at the last, Helka unleashed her most devastating runes to destroy the pass along with many dragons, though the rune magic also took the lives of Helka and the brave Dwarves who stood with her that final day. The Dwarves found no refuge in the rolling, treeless hills and steep ravines that bordered the Molten Heath to the southwest. Eventually their wanderings led them to a vast mountain chain: some journeyed east, forming the settlements of the Jornall Clan, while others continued traveling south, building the city of Yrthwright's Forge beside a volcano in the heart of a bountiful valley, named as a reminder of the glory of their former kingdom. Valnir and many of her people, however, built homes amongst the mist-shrouded peaks that would become the Dunwarr Mountains, driven underground by the occasional dragon still flying out of the north until they left the sky behind entirely and called their new home the Dunwarr, or "sanctuary." The children of Valnir became the first Deeplords, protecting and leading their people. Sources The Early History of the Dwarves (Tales of Darkness), pp. 30–31 Black Ember Gorge (The Molten Heath), p. 194 The Karok Doum (The Molten Heath), p. 194

title: Herman's Gulch
content: Herman's Gulch Herman's Gulch is a settlement on the banks of the Weeping Scar River, the farthest inland location to which seagoing vessels can sail into Zanaga, and the largest foreign settlement on the continent. The path to Herman's Gulch from the ocean is a long and winding one, but it is the only way through the leagues of swamps that shield Zanaga's shores. Small by the standards of most towns of Terrinoth, it is nonetheless from here that Humans and other daring visitors begin their journey into the unknown. In a cave beneath the town, the spider goddess Arachne controls her secret empire. Sources A New World (Zanaga), pp. 252–255

title: Hernfar Isle
content: Hernfar Isle Hernfar Isle sits where the Lothan River is at its widest, the furthest eastern outpost of the Daqan Lords and home to the garrison of Hernfar Keep. The isle is deceptively unremarkable, with little to distinguish it from any other common river island save its proximity to the Ru Steppes — a few vermin, some light birdsong on the breeze — but this very semblance of calm keeps its garrison on edge. Soldiers posted there find that shadows seem longer or flicker strangely in the light, and no few have tales of luminescent eyes staring from across the water; on nights when the moon is heavy and red, some say a cacophony of howls and screams rises across the water that few can confidently attribute to mere animals. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Hernfar Keep
content: Hernfar Keep Hernfar Keep is the garrison on Hernfar Isle, the furthest eastern outpost of the Daqan Lords in Kell. Recruits to the Kell militia often joke that their commanders are the harshest in all Terrinoth, for insubordination is punished with an assignment to Hernfar's garrison. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: High Hall
content: High Hall The High Hall overlooks the cliff edge of Lagart; its roof is the upturned Axe of Isheim, a mighty vessel said to have carried the first Weik to their frozen home. Sources The Frozen North (Isheim), p. 233

title: Highmont
content: Highmont Highmont is the home of Baroness Adelynn of Forthyn, from which she personally oversees the raising and training of the barony's famed rocs. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Hiresh
content: Hiresh Hiresh, the Prince of Coin, is perhaps the most influential of the Caliph's advisors, although Jorgul, the Spear of the Desert, often challenges this claim. Hiresh often speaks in the Caliph's stead, and it is to this wizened pennypincher that the viziers and collegiate deans must bend a knee if they wish to petition for the capital's aid. Intensely paranoid, Hiresh is never without a cloud of bodyguards; he even employs numerous body doubles for his protection, which has given him a reputation for being everywhere at once. Heroes who involve themselves in the goings-on of the palace are as likely to encounter Hiresh as either an ally or an enemy — the Prince of Coin is always interested in individuals willing to spread his influence or enact his will beyond the city walls. Such individuals should be wary, however, for Hiresh can turn from friend to foe as swiftly as a desert wind might rise from the sands, especially if it serves his purpose to have others take the blame for his misdeeds. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), pp. 243–244

title: Horn of Courage
content: Horn of Courage Horns play an important role in the mythology of the Weik, for they state that the gods themselves blow war horns when preparing for battle. This horn, made from a cracked, ancient cattle horn and banded with bright silver, is rumored to have been made by priests of Nordros, and certainly attests to their myths. When an adventurer blows the horn, their allies are filled with encouragement and inspiration; the horn is also very loud, and under most circumstances can be easily heard by all characters and creatures out to extreme range, and likely farther. Sources Magic Items, p. 109

title: Host of Thorns
content: Host of Thorns The Host of Thorns was Llovar's renewed army in the final years of the First Darkness, so great it was said to blacken the face of the world, gathered in the distant Ru Darklands after the loss of his Orcish allies left him able to rely only on Warlord Hellspanth's dragons. Llovar split the Host into several contingents, each led by a trusted lieutenant whose names soon became bywords for wickedness and treachery: the bone-witch Q'aro Fenn, Melinesh the Cruel and Terrible, Nashaia King's Bane, and Kul the Serpent. In 487, the Host of Thorns invaded Talindon, sweeping all before it and slaying King Falladir Penacor and his sons at The Ashen Field, before finally being broken and routed at the Battle of the Locusts. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 36–37

title: House Crosta
content: House Crosta House Crosta was one of three rebellious cousins' factions, alongside House Varnii and House Ferastii, that opposed Emperor Gentias II of House Harthorn during Lorimor's civil war of 1485–1490. At the Battle of Ranthor Bay in 1490, Gentias II tricked House Crosta and House Varnii into believing House Ferastii wished to combine their forces there; in the resulting surprise assault, the head of House Crosta was killed, ending the civil war. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), pp. 49–50

title: House Dalibor
content: House Dalibor House Dalibor is the vampiric noble house that rules Castle Dalibor within The Mistlands, currently led by Kyndrithul. Sources Castle Dalibor (The Mistlands), p. 161

title: House Ferastii
content: House Ferastii House Ferastii was one of three rebellious cousins' factions, alongside House Varnii and House Crosta, that opposed Emperor Gentias II of House Harthorn during Lorimor's civil war of 1485–1490. At the Battle of Ranthor Bay in 1490, once news of House Crosta's defeat and House Varnii's capture reached the head of House Ferastii, he abandoned his cause and fled into exile, ending the civil war. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), pp. 49–50

title: House Harthorn
content: House Harthorn House Harthorn is a noble house descended from the fecund line of Emperor Viason I of Lorimor, holding the imperial throne through Emperors Derisian IV and Gentias II. House Harthorn's rivalries with House Varnii, House Crosta, and House Ferastii plunged Lorimor into a civil war beginning in 1485, ultimately won by Gentias II at the Battle of Ranthor Bay in 1490 — after which House Harthorn liquidated House Varnii's possessions in The Torue Albes, provoking the revolts that led to Lutetia Dallia's founding of the Queendom of the Torue Albes. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), pp. 49–50

title: House Varnii
content: House Varnii House Varnii is a noble house descended from the fecund line of Emperor Viason I of Lorimor, rivals of House Harthorn whose distant branch briefly held the young Emperor Viason III in the Torue Albes in 1315. During the civil war of 1485–1490, House Varnii was one of three rebellious cousins' factions opposing Emperor Gentias II, its head taken in chains after the Battle of Ranthor Bay. In the war's aftermath, House Harthorn liquidated House Varnii's possessions in The Torue Albes, everything of value pawned or looted for the empire's benefit — a betrayal that provoked the islanders' revolts and ultimately led to Lutetia Dallia's founding of the independent Queendom of the Torue Albes. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), pp. 49–50

title: Hrgrun
content: Hrgrun Hrgrun was an Orc spiritspeaker of the lost expedition that vanished into Zanaga before the Second Darkness, ancestor of Urgash the Pitiless, who still wears Hrgrun's glowing magical crystal around his bloodstained neck. Sources The Lost Expedition (Zanaga), p. 255

title: Hyrrinx
content: Hyrrinx The Hyrrinx are a compact breed of Catfolk with lynx-like tall ears and a bobbed tail, found in desolate areas across Terrinoth and Dunwarr, among the best hunters and trackers in all of Mennara — the name also belongs to a small Hyrrinx village nestled within Eventide Forest, mostly isolated from the surrounding barony of Allerfeldt. Society Each small Hyrrinx village is governed by a council of elders. When food runs scarce, as is often the case in winters, the village exiles adults who are unmarried, less productive, or have run afoul of the reigning council — these exiles are called Rythkin. Hyrrinx culture is otherwise based on communal simplicity: food is shared, all aid in village upkeep and building dens, and trades are designed so that the needs of all are met, with those who cannot hunt expected to develop a skill that provides for the tribe. Although a baron officially has claim over all people living in their territory under Citadel law, the Sephone line has historically allowed the community of Hyrrinx in Eventide Forest to govern itself independently and remain untaxed, a status quo Baroness Katrin has thus far maintained. Alongside the residents of Dragonholt, the Hyrrinx regard the Tree of Tales within the forest as sacred. Sources Catfolk and Half-Catfolk (Character Species), p. 68 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Hysshari Brotherhoods
content: Hysshari Brotherhoods The Hysshari Brotherhoods are cults of murder that serve the Caliph and their viziers, training assassins in hidden mountain temples and oasis fortresses across Al-Kalim. At the Tower of Knives, which hangs like a dagger from the cavern roof of Haruun, acrobatic killers master the arts of wall walking. In the Valley of Ash, Brotherhood members train with mysterious bladewomen to learn the secrets of silent killing and night fighting. Sources Life in the Sands (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Ice Storm Rune
content: Ice Storm Rune Ice storm runes can be used to create a localized but very intense blizzard, requiring no moisture and functioning even in arid environments — a bearer who activates such a rune quickly becomes the epicenter of a swirling vortex of snow-blown wind that can be directed to move independently of the wielder, anyone caught within soon suffering the effects of freezing cold. As a weapon, the ice storm rune is particularly effective against Dragonkin, many of whom regard the bearers of such runes with fear and hatred. Lord Roland of Kell famously bore an ice storm runebound shard in his duel against the Dragonlord Margath. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 118 The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 47–48

title: Ice Wyrm
content: Ice Wyrm As cold as the lands in which they crawl, ice wyrms are truly beings of ice and snow, dimly related to the great dragons of ancient times and creations of the Rime Storm, their blood cold enough to freeze flesh. Covered in glittering diamond scales, each like a huge icy mirror, ice wyrms move across the snow, dazzling enemies just before they strike. Long, icicle-like fangs and wickedly sharp claws make swift work of their victims, while the wyrms' spines are sharp enough to slice a Human in two. Ice wyrms, like their dragon ancestors, are deeply dangerous foes, conversant in many dark tongues; these beings have enslaved or bargained with most of the monstrous races of the north, enlisting them in their unending war against the remnants of the Salishwyrd. Many grow great wings of cold leather, and silently glide over the glaciers in search of prey; some ice wyrms even practice sorcery and are able to spit spells as well as streams of freezing blood. Scarsha the Vile, Queen of the ice wyrms, is perhaps the most deadly of her kind. Sources Life in the Cold (Isheim), p. 237

title: Ice-Blood Warrior
content: Ice-Blood Warrior The White Death is an insidious effect of the Rime Storm that can claim those unfortunates who traverse Isheim's northern wilds. For some, the White Death merely kills, leaving their frozen corpses contorted in their final moments of death. For others, it can be even worse, transmuting their once-warm blood into icy fluid. Their veins filled with sorcerous cold, they become sadistic killers, preying upon any being or creature that crosses their path. Raging and cursing, these frozen beings are drawn to the warmth of hot-blooded creatures so they might quench the heat with their eternal cold; fighting off such adversaries is a terrible struggle, even their touch can blacken flesh with frostbite. As the cold does not affect them anymore, wild clans of ice-blood warriors plague the silent forests and endless tundra of the north, their white eyes unblinking as they search for warm prey. Like that of Ice Wyrms and Wendigo, their blood has value; further, rumor has it that there is magic that can bring an individual back from this icy fate, giving hope to those who have lost loved ones to the White Death. Sources Life in the Cold (Isheim), pp. 237–238

title: Ice-Blood
content: Ice-Blood Ice-blood is the vital fluid of rare northern creatures of Isheim like the Wendigo and the Ice Wyrms, perpetually cold and prized for many uses in the south, from elixirs to quell fevers to weapons that can slay with a touch. It was the discovery of ice-blood that made fortunes for Weik hunters, alongside more mundane exports like whale oil, seawyrm blubber, and hardy frostholm timber. The Hearthlords now vie among themselves for control of these resources, sometimes using manipulation and politics, at other times raids and open warfare. Sources Lords of the Hearth (Isheim), p. 234

title: Icegate Prison
content: Icegate Prison Icegate Prison is a frozen tomb high in the World's End Mountains, one of the few structures to remain above the snow of The White Death. Once the place where the Salishwyrd Elves incarcerated the worst of their kind and the most dangerous of their foes, it has become a lair for tormented souls and coiling horrors. Here, the queen of the ice wyrms, Scarsha, rules; the prison is a lair for her many offspring, and from it she wages her war against the last of the Salishwyrd. Sources Realm of the White Death (Isheim), p. 236

title: Ilendar
content: Ilendar Captain Ilendar commands the rank and file of the Latari army in Lithelin. While noble blood is required to become an officer, Ilendar accepts into the ranks all who can meet the physical requirements of soldiering, including Verdelam who have failed to ascend within Elven society. Sources Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Immolation Rune
content: Immolation Rune Immolation runes are weapons in and of themselves — when activated, a burst of flame projects forward from the rune. These runes have their own source of power, but a user can concentrate some of their own energies into increasing the size and intensity of the flames, injurious to the user but far more so to their target. The burst only lasts for a few seconds, so the shards are useless for illumination, but they are effective for personal protection and starting fires. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), pp. 118–119

title: Ingunn Vergsbold
content: Ingunn Vergsbold Ingunn Vergsbold was the head of the Masons' Guild in Thelgrim who, in the Age of Courage, set out to rebuild the city's long-destroyed districts in the aftermath of the Third Darkness, and who rose to become the first First Speaker of the Dunwarr Guilds. Her reconstruction effort continued for decades, and she did not stop at rebuilding: calling on what remained of Thelgrim's noble wealth, she had the Miners' Guild cut the great chasm linking Thelgrim to the Hearth Road that leads to the outside world, while the Merchants' Guild partnered with the Miners' and Explorers' Guild to reestablish ties with the other Dunwarr holds. As trade and travel increased along the reopened road, so did the power of the Guilds; many noble families who had refused to invest in the rebuilding lost their estates in Thelgrim to the Guilds' expansion. By 1550 the Guilds ruled Dunwarr in all but name, and within two more decades had codified the laws governing the election of Dunwarr's speakers from among the Guildmasters — with Ingunn Vergsbold becoming the first to hold the title of First Speaker. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 50–51

title: Ironbound
content: Ironbound The Ironbound are living suits of armor made of black iron, created by the Priests of Pollux in Nerekhall to be beyond the corruption of mortal beings and immune to magic both malign and beneficial, out of fear of ever again falling to the lure of the Ynfernael. These constructs exceeded the expectations of the artificers who made them and soon replaced most of Nerekhall's militia; today they are a common sight on the city's streets, safeguarding the citizenry against flagrant acts of evil magic, and those who claim to have witnessed one malfunction or fail are harshly punished for spreading malicious rumors. Armed with long spears and heavy shields and covered in armor plates bearing special runic wards granting further immunity to destructive magic, the Ironbound are Terrinoth's strongest response to its magic-wielding enemies, though they lack initiative and drive and can often be defeated through cunning and ingenuity — a fact useful to travelers who run afoul of Nerekhall's many laws against uncivil behavior or its antimagic ordinances. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 148 Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), p. 153

title: Irram
content: Irram Perched on the edge of the Desert of Eternity, Irram is the oldest of Al-Kalim's cities aside from the capital Al-Madena, one of the four vizier city-states. Its master, the Sun Priestess Sharish, is both leader of her people and custodian of the Grand Temple of A'tar. Irram is a center of religion and worship, and pilgrims travel from across the Caliphate to pray in its many shrines. In the middle of its sprawling tangle of ancient sandstone buildings stands the tomb of the first Caliph; once each Caliph's reign is over, their body is brought here baked in clay, so it might be entombed within their likeness forever. Irram is often in conflict with the Collegiate Arcane, and its own conclave of wizards has little power within the city walls, for Sharish believes that the fruits of Djinn magic are intrinsically tainted, and she would see the Caliphate's reliance upon them ended — a stance that also brings her into opposition with other viziers who see only the wealth ancient Djinn artifacts can bring. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 245

title: Isheim
content: Isheim Isheim is a frozen wilderness perched on the edge of the world, across the roiling northern seas from Terrinoth, where cold skies heavy with snow and sleet press down upon the land and a keening wind howls forth from ice-clad peaks. Overview Isheim is the lost land of the Salishwyrd, ancient Elves who ruled this continent before years of hunger and darkness turned their paradise into a frozen nightmare. Beneath the snow and ice, the glories of their northern empire still hide, hunted by heroes and fought over by scheming ice wyrms and savage Hearthlords. Heroes traveling to this remote land might find themselves caught up in the Weik lords' trade wars, delve into the secret depths of the volcanic city of Vrede, or join an expedition of ice-blood hunters as they seek out frozen beasts. The paths of the most daring could even take them far beyond the coastal cities and settlements, past the lands of the Onoit and the lairs of the ice wyrms, to discover the ruins of the Elven empire and perhaps even The Green Vale, last city of the Salishwyrd. The land is divided between The Raider's Coast of the Weik, the middle wilderness roamed by the Onoit, and the far north known as The White Death. Sources Isheim (Chapter III - Lands of Magic), p. 232

title: Jade Glen
content: Jade Glen The Jade Glen is a range of hills in Eastern Terrinoth, offering the region's people a peaceful respite from the bleak landscape of the nearby Borderlands. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Jararr
content: Jararr Jararr is the great panther god of the Wild Hunt, vicious brother of Hamzah the Pridelord. Hunters of Zanaga offer this ferocious figure of blood and death prayers before the kill and raise gore-streaked obsidian statues in his honor. Whereas Hamzah stands for civilization and tribe, Jararr is a loner; among the Singhara, the worship of Jararr is practiced by outcasts who choose to dye their manes black in deference to their brutal master. Adventurers seek out Jararr that they might hunt at the great panther's side, for if they can keep pace with the giant beast and bring down his quarry, a measure of the kill can be theirs. Equally, evil Singhara potionmasters have been known to place Jararr's prey mark upon their enemies. Sources A New World (Zanaga), p. 254

title: Jatok
content: Jatok Jatok, the Water Temple, is a former lizardman temple now a nest of naga power in Zanaga, a sunken tomb into which all of Zanaga's rivers eventually flow. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Jendra's Harbor
content: Jendra's Harbor Jendra's Harbor is the most prosperous city of the barony of Telor, seated on the southern side of Kingless Bay where the river of Korina's Tears meets the sea. The port is one of the few reliable landings for ships arriving from across the sea, hosting travelers from Lorimor and as far as Al-Kalim, and serves as a departure point for ships bound for the Torue Albes or, occasionally, Zanaga. Though Baron Echard officially rules Telor, Countess Sela's stewardship of the harbor has granted her greater influence throughout Terrinoth and beyond. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Jenti the Just
content: Jenti the Just Jenti the Just was a sightless sorcerer of the Lorimor Imperial Court who, aided by a Vision Rune, overcame unhealable injuries to become a famed figure at court. [not stated in source: no further biographical detail is given] Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 121

title: Jer'Kul Urak
content: Jer'Kul Urak The Jer'Kul, or "Lower-Dwellers," live most of their lives within The Kul Valleys, the wide valleys formed when earthquakes split The Broken Plains apart across hundreds of leagues. Unlike most of the other Orc tribes, this tribe relies on agriculture and animal husbandry to survive. Its members grow crops on small plots of valley land, which they tend and harvest as they roam across the Kul with herds of small elk, jarn deer, and other wildlife that long ago fell into the valleys and evolved to exist here. Most other Orc tribes look down on the Jer'Kul (literally), but the valley-dwellers make intricate metalworks of silver that many view as blessed by the spirits of the underworld. It is possible their beliefs could be true, but not as they imagine — there are vents in some of the valleys where some hear dark whispers and can make out terrible visages floating in the choking smoke that emerges from the ground. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 200

title: Jerem Camford
content: Jerem Camford Baron Jerem Camford led a force ambushed by undead cavalry at the Battle of Ramscrossing while negotiating a swollen river during the Second Darkness. When Camford ordered a retreat, Ardus Ix'Erebus's Deathborn forces harried his troops so brutally that they were in no state to defend their lands upon regrouping; the Deathborn Legion soon fell upon the Barony of Camford in force, utterly ravaging it and slaughtering the baron and his heirs. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 41

title: Jerlon Penacor
content: Jerlon Penacor King Jerlon Penacor came to the throne of Talindon in 286 showing every sign of proving worthy of the crown, his capable queen Riya celebrated at court for her intelligence and charm, and their infant sons Farrengol and Farrendon showing every sign of becoming fine princes of the Penacor line. History Love tore the realm apart, however. Queen Riya and the king's greatest friend and highest councilor, Rusticar Lorimor, had fallen deeply for each other despite their respective vows to husband and throne; when the king learned of this, his priests and advisors begged him to show no clemency, but Jerlon still loved his queen and grew melancholic rather than wrathful. He annulled his marriage and forever banished Riya and Rusticar from the kingdom — a large group of the king's subjects joined them in exile, a happenstance that led some to wonder if there was more to the betrayal than mere love, and that Jerlon had trouble commanding the loyalty of his subjects. Rusticar and Riya went on to found the Lorimor Empire on the shores of the western ocean. In Talindon, Jerlon lamented his lost love and refused to countenance taking another queen; behind his back, his courtiers began to call him the King of Grief. His remaining son Farrengol, lacking any parental hand with his mother exiled and his father lost to melancholy, fell in with coarser members of the household guard and was eventually condemned to death by his own father for the crimes of the outlaw band he had formed — Farrengol would later return from death as the undead lord Farrenghast.
